GRB afterglows exhibit distinct behaviors, shifting abruptly when the jet breaks due to radiative losses in ultra-relativistic phases or radiation from shocks in non-relativistic phases, yet modeling these processes separately can result in overlapping, yet inaccessible, regions. This paper presents a new model that unifies afterglow phenomena across all momentum components, accounting for the transition between ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic phases. By incorporating multiple particle distributions and relativistic shock radiation, we derive a comprehensive equation that encompasses all phases and observes the anticipated break and continuum in spectral signals. Furthermore, this paper includes derivations for broad-band color-evolution, all-electron energy reconnection events, and radiation from shocks in the non-relativistic phase, with predictive formulas for observed spectral characteristics across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from gamma-rays to radio waves, for all phases and jet components.

A bipartite graph can be rendered as a non-overlapping, layered drawing on a plane if its maximum vertex degree exceeds 2, by breaking certain edge connections and rearranging them in a chain structure. The process, known as "splitting vertices," essentially divides specific vertices into multiple parts, each corresponding to a distinct level in the layered drawing. A key observation in this study shows that a bipartite graph with a maximum vertex degree greater than two can be represented as a non-overlapping, layered drawing on a plane, by splitting specific vertices and reassigning the connections between them, without needing any additional edge breaking. The proposed method also provides a constructive algorithm for creating such a representation, which includes the identification of vertices to be split and a step-by-step guide on how to carry out the edge reassignments.

This study explores the benefits of automated feedback control for bipedal robots in their gait cycles, using a highly structured and predictable simulation environment. By comparing closed-loop and open-loop versions of the same robot, our findings show that even without precise initial conditions, closed-loop feedback ensures consistent gait performance, prevents deviations from the desired state, and reduces the impact of external disturbances. In addition, the study reveals that the effectiveness of closed-loop control is unaffected by changes in walking speed, a key aspect of bipedal robots. The proposed approach also enables the incorporation of sensory input and more efficient energy recovery, further enhancing bipedal robot performance.

This work provides an infinite field k as the base field for the power series field K, consisting of power series with coefficients in k. We examine the properties and variations of the power series field K, particularly equipping it with a total residue map, and show that this results in a residued complete discrete valuation field. We also investigate the decidability of this power series field, revealing that it has a computably presentable theory if and only if the base field k has a computably presentable theory. We further establish that if k serves as a base field for the polynomial ring and has a certain property, namely being of characteristic zero and having a computably decidible theory, then the associated power series field will also have this property.

Memory-resident functions, a common target for attacks, can now be compromised 
easily due to the effectiveness of Flush+Reload attacks. In order to enhance the 
precision and efficiency of these attacks, we present HyperDegrade, an enhanced 
version of memory-degrading techniques. By utilizing HyperDegrade, it is possible 
to execute memory-resident functions at a significantly higher resolution, with 
a hundred times greater time accuracy and the requirement for a hundred times 
fewer traces compared to existing methods. Additionally, HyperDegrade's improved 
performance is achievable on regular hardware, without the need for any 
modifications. We demonstrate the enhanced effectiveness of HyperDegrade through 
successful Flush+Reload attacks on regular x86-64 systems running popular operating 
systems, and showcase the potential of this technique by compromising the 
memory of a system remotely, using a publicly available web application as the 
attack vector.

Isotopy classes of certain knotted structures, specifically 4-cycles in a 3-dimensional space, have been organized into a comprehensive framework based on their projection patterns. This framework, initially outlined in a previous study, enables the identification of a specific set of movements called diagonal moves. These diagonal moves can transform one knotted 4-cycle into another, while the corresponding linked pair of knots remains unchanged. It has been observed that a particular type of knotted structure, the (1,1)-torus knot, can be reached from any given knotted 4-cycle through a sequence of these diagonal moves. This process is achieved by concatenating a series of closed loops of knot types (p,q) with the parameters p and q adding up to 2, which can then be dissolved into a single (1,1)-torus knot. This discovery can be utilized to develop a more refined understanding of the relationship between knotted 4-cycles and (1,1)-torus knots.

We establish a connection between a specific class of cocycles and the Jones polynomial's variational properties. By demonstrating that a substantial subset of its variants can be obtained through integration of these cocycles, we show their invariance under modification of the knot's projection. This discovery leads to a topological interpretation of the 4-cocycle whose cohomology class corresponds to the $sl_2$ quantum invariant, as it generates a change in the knot's underlying topological properties. This finding also explains the recent observation made in recent studies on the subject.

We set up a new performance metric for task allocation in multi-agent systems based on variable difficulty levels and agent capabilities, and then leverage existing optimization techniques to provide a comparative analysis of different optimization approaches for task allocation in this complex scenario. Our findings, obtained through numerical experiments, reveal that the distribution of task difficulties and agent capabilities has a distinct impact on the effectiveness of different optimization methods in achieving high performance in multi-agent systems. Interestingly, our results also show that the performance of the best optimization approach can degrade significantly in scenarios where there is a large disparity in task difficulty levels, despite its overall superiority. To address this performance decline, we propose a modified optimization method that adapts to changing environments and find that this adaptation leads to a significant improvement in the performance of the best optimization approach in such challenging scenarios.

This study reveals critical security vulnerabilities in current vertical federated learning methods, revealing that sensitive information from training data is inadvertently revealed due to incomplete privacy protections in protocols and algorithms. Using the vertical federated learning setup with Florida and Texas data sets, our research shows that both statistical attacks and pure privacy attacks can successfully extract delicate features from training sets, compromising security and confidentiality. To address this issue, we propose an enhanced method called Federated Learning with Partial Confidentiality, demonstrating significant improvements in protecting privacy and securing confidentiality, as evidenced by our comprehensive experiments with real-world data sets.

Neural network training data can be efficiently handled by reducing the dimensionality of input features while maintaining predictive accuracy, which facilitates processing large datasets and enhances computational efficiency. Random Fourier Features (RFF) is a widely adopted method for constructing pseudo features from input data, obviating the need to store and process extensive, high-dimensional data. However, RFF has notable limitations, primarily stemming from the non-deterministic nature of its feature generation process, which results in suboptimal performance compared to the original data. To address this challenge, we present Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a novel, probabilistic method that generates a fixed set of features with a specified probability distribution, leading to a significant decrease in the required number of features while achieving superior performance, particularly in low-dimensional settings. We compare the performance of PRFF and RFF on synthetic and real-world datasets and demonstrate improved accuracy and a greater feature dimension reduction ratio in favor of PRFF.

This paper introduces Cartesian Decomposition, a new concept that allows us to break down the diagonal group within a regular group action into its constituent parts. The name is inspired by the "Cartesian Connected Component" technique used in the analysis of dynamical systems. A key feature of Cartesian Decomposition is that it automatically yields a diagonal group for each regular group action. Conversely, any diagonal group can be framed within an appropriate regular group action. Along the way, this paper reveals an unanticipated connection between regular group actions and the graph of their associated dynamical systems. A regular group action's ability to preserve a horizontal field also leads to the identification of an associated horizontal form through the use of invariant sections. This form can be further characterized as a leafwise 1-form on the system's leaves. Next, the paper shows how the Cartesian Decomposition framework can be used to replicate the process of obtaining the Euler-Lagrange operator from a regular group action, thus providing a more general understanding of this process. A comprehensive discussion on the relationship between the Euler-Lagrange operator, the diagonal group, and the horizontal form reveals that any of these three components can be used to determine the others. This paper ultimately demonstrates that the Euler-Lagrange operator, the diagonal group, and the horizontal form all share a common underlying structure, accessible through the lens of regular group actions. This structure, in turn, forms the basis for a sophisticated characterization of coherent spaces in the context of regular group actions.

We establish the existence of compact conformally flat hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space of dimensions five and above, with specified scalar curvature, and bounded by a smooth surface of constant positive curvature.

This study introduces a novel Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique (GAST) for fixed low-power transmission networks without channel information at the mobile device. By dynamically switching between multiple antennas, GAST enhances energy efficiency by allocating power more equitably between transmission and reception. The analysis indicates that the GAST's optimal performance occurs when the antenna-switching pattern is symmetrical, resulting in a higher throughput and a more even power distribution between transmission and reception. The proposed GAST is compared to a single-antenna configuration with time division between transmission and reception, demonstrating significant performance improvements, including an increased throughput of up to 6.85 times and a reduced drop in signal-to-noise ratio of up to 5.58 dB.

The spread of influence through social networks is a subject of growing interest, particularly as it relates to the resilience of these networks. A recent study analyzed the impact of random node removals in large networks that have undergone significant disturbance, specifically looking at the effects of a single removal on networks that have experienced widespread influence spread, or "epidemics". The study's findings, published in an earlier study, revealed that the network's fragmentation could be understood using a simple probabilistic model, where the probability of a node connecting to another is determined by the relative distance between the two, based on their placement within the network. The study aimed to explore how this network fragmentation changes when a single node is removed, either rapidly or slowly, in networks of varying sizes. The study discovered that the spread of influence often results in small groups of closely connected nodes, and when a single node is removed quickly, the fragmentation process is similar to rolling a dice, with the outcome determining the network's configuration, especially if the network has an odd number of nodes. The study found that the average distance between nodes in a network that has experienced influence spread increases with the network size, adhering to a specific growth pattern. Here, a novel, highly sensitive interferometer concept is presented, which significantly enhances the-carrier-noise ratio by employing a specific geometric arrangement. By optimizing this setup, a remarkable improvement of up to $10^{5}$ in the carrier-to-noise ratio can be achieved, exceeding the limitations of traditional interferometers by several orders of magnitude. Specifically, the proposed sloshing-Sagnac interferometer exhibits improved performance, with a carrier-to-noise ratio of $10^{5}$ attainable for photon numbers as low as 10, demonstrating a marked improvement over the conventional Sagnac interferometer. This breakthrough design, which leverages a unique geometric configuration to amplify the effect of carrier phase noise, levers a specific nonlinear interaction between the input and output light within a microring resonator. This phenomenon is critically dependent on the precise alignment of light beams, thereby eliminating unwanted noise sources and allowing the interferometer to operate with reduced loss.

This paper proposes a new random access (RA) protocol called NOVR-XL for large-scale millimeter wave (XL-MIMO) systems. XL-MIMO systems face significant interference challenges due to simultaneous transmissions from multiple users, making random access a critical issue. Existing RA protocols are designed for small-MIMO systems and often result in low success rates. In contrast, NOVR-XL is specifically tailored to support simultaneous transmissions in XL-MIMO and leverages the time and frequency resources occupied by these transmissions to enhance random access efficiency. By doing so, NOVR-XL achieves a 94.5% increase in successful RA attempts and a 37.7% reduction in required time compared to the conventional time division multiple access protocol.

A protoplanetary disk's inner region is thought to be the source of planetary formation, and by studying its evolution, we can understand how planets, including Earth, were formed. While the established theory of gravitational instability suggests that substructures in the disk's inner region could lead to the formation of solid particles through a process known as streaming instability, it's unclear how these structures would persist and where particles would accumulate to form planetesimals. Using numerical simulations of a disk with a gap, we discovered the presence of a persistent accumulation zone where particles could become stuck and eventually form planetesimals, fueling different formation mechanisms for both rocky and icy planets at different radii. By examining the temperature and pressure patterns in the simulation, we found that a particular structure, a dust trap near the star, would facilitate the formation of small planets, while a more stable accumulation zone, located farther from the star, would give rise to larger planets through gravitational instability in pebbles. By comparing our results to observations of the TW Haeze, we believe that the protoplanetary disk in this simulation is similar to the inner region of a disk that could potentially form a planetary system resembling our own.

A comprehensive microscopically-based energy density functional, dubbed BigApple, has been thoroughly tested for a vast range of heavy radon and lead nuclei with various deformations. Theoretical predictions from BigApple, especially regarding nuclear radius and spinodal density, were compared to experimental outcomes, demonstrating excellent agreement. Specifically, the distribution of radius parameters across the studied range holds a standard deviation of 1.56%, while the mean and standard deviation of spinodal densities exhibit a small deviation from empirical values. Notably, BigApple predictions for the nuclear level density parameter (i.e., $a_v = 31.75 \pm 0.75$ MeV) also align well with previous cluster model estimates and the empirical value inferred from collective states in even-even rare earth and actinide nuclei. Utilizing BigApple, we derived the energy density functional Skyrme-like form with corresponding parameters, which were validated through various tests to ensure their reliability. Consequently, BigApple has been successfully applied to investigate key properties of nuclear matter at the saturation point, including isothermal bulk compression modulus, nuclear surface, and Coulomb-like screening length. By calibrating the BigApple energy density functional with respect to the equation of state of nuclear matter at saturation density, we mapped out the parameter space of the BigApple functional and correlated these parameters with physical properties of representative radon and lead nuclei, providing a comprehensive understanding of the BigApple functional's behavior.

Our study examines the performance of Molmer-Sorensen gates under frequency errors, particularly for a specific implementation using trapped ions. We demonstrate that close-proximity entanglement generation can be extremely robust to frequency drifts, with a metric indicating robustness showing a cubic relationship with the number of ions. This phenomenon is attributed to a unique balancing of entangling and disentangling dynamics during the gate execution. Our findings suggest that robust Molmer-Sorensen gates can serve as a key component for a large-scale, frequency-stable quantum processor.

A recently discovered material, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$, exhibits both Dirac electrons and strong many-body physics, presenting an intriguing combination that is both rare and not well understood. This study delves into the electronic properties of this material, revealing a highly correlated Dirac metal state that is both rare and complex, and is likely to display unique phenomena such as a Kondo insulator or a magnetic metal state. To further study this material's properties, a comprehensive theoretical framework is established through a combination of an orbital-driven spin-orbit coupling with strong on-site Coulomb repulsion, and many-body physics is then studied with this framework, with results that potentially explain the material's experimental features such as its magnetic behavior and electronic structure.

The potential of the LHC and future experiments at $e^+ e-$, $e^+ p$, $pp$, and $p$p$)$ colliders to detect heavy neutral leptons with masses beyond 1 TeV has been thoroughly examined in a comprehensive study. By applying optimized search techniques for different lepton flavors and taking into consideration existing limits from other experiments, future experiments can significantly enhance the minimal supersymmetric standard model's detection capabilities by up to three orders of magnitude. At the mu$^+$ mu$^{-}$ collider with 1 TeV energy and luminosity of 10 ab$^{-1}$, the detection limit can be as low as 1 ten-millionth of the muon neutrino field. Similar detection limits can be achieved at the 100 TeV hadron colliders with the same lepton flavor, while the 1 TeV electron-positron collider with the same energy and luminosity can detect heavy neutral leptons with masses up to 3 TeV in some scenarios.

This paper introduces a new neural language model called the Spiking Neural Language Model, which generates words based on the most likely previous word to have preceded them, in contrast to traditional neural language models that estimate the probability of each word given historical context. By paring this model with a grammar-based precursor, we've developed a hybrid method that boosts the performance of basic N-gram models and provides significant enhancements in low-data scenarios, particularly in machine translation and summarization. Specifically, our research found that combining a spiking neural language model with a 4-gram model achieved state-of-the-art results in WMT 2014 French-to-English news translation, even without using extensive training data. Additionally, our hybrid method demonstrated enhanced performance over current state-of-the-art baselines in two summarization datasets. The code for our research is available online at: https://github.com/ghrua/SNLM.

Reconstructing a 3D face relies heavily on modeling its two-dimensional projections from various viewing angles. Previous approaches divide the representation into separate components, including a low-dimensional face code and a view-dependent factor, often trained independently and then coupled through a neural network in a single-dimensional representation. In contrast, The Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet) splits the representation into two separate, dual-component codes that are coupled through two distinct view-dependent factors for the x and y-axes. By doing so, it leverages the inherent symmetry in the relationship between front and side views of the face. Rather than projecting view-dependent factors onto the sphere, the method uses a facial mesh as a manifold for predicting the face. In its current form, the model is able to create a 3D face from two projections from different viewing angles, with an orientation that is completely aligned with the facial structure.

Researchers have discovered specific scenarios of inflationary dynamics leading to unusually large negative values of the Bardeen potential, a phenomenon that could contribute to the formation of large-scale power in the cosmic density field. This occurrence is associated with a sharp increase in the power in the scalar field fluctuations at a particular small scale, a phenomenon that may arise from the sudden formation of a quantum field state during inflation. In this work, a previously unexplored mechanism for this state formation process is presented, which involves a sudden change in the type of inflation, such as an eternal inflation transition or a phase transition, causing a sharp increase in the curvature of space-time and, as a result, an abrupt growth of a minimal wavelength of fluctuations that can survive until the end of inflation, with immediate consequences for the distribution of the Bardeen potential.

Researchers compared the number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees and marked ordered trees under specific conditions. They defined a function $f_n$ that counts the number of deepest nodes in trees of size $n$ and discovered that this function behaves differently for standard and marked ordered trees. Through explicit formula derivations, they found that the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees is approximately $2.44158n^{d-2}$, where $d$ is the minimum number of ancestors a node can have, which is typically $2$ in binary trees. In contrast, the corresponding value for marked ordered trees is approximately $1.5$ times the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees with the same distribution of ancestor numbers.

The accuracy of optical character recognition in vote tabulation can be affected by the incorrect spelling of candidate names. Our research aims to enhance the reliability of this technology by developing a spell correction algorithm specifically for this context. Due to the large number of incorrect spellings, a single-scanner spell checker is not a suitable solution, as it would require a dictionary of considerable size that would either necessitate an excessively large training data set or an impractically long list of common words in voting scenarios. Consequently, a page-based spell checker is proposed, where the spell correction is performed on a page-by-page basis rather than a word-by-word approach. This algorithm utilizes the $K$-nearest neighbors method in combination with a simple character n-gram model to achieve effective spell correction. The efficacy of this algorithm is evaluated using a voting data set containing over 50,000 incorrect spellings and 20,000 correct spellings, and the results show that it is capable of accurately identifying and correcting incorrect spellings even when the spellers do not consistently maintain the same level of accuracy. The proposed algorithm is a practical solution that can be applied to voting scenarios and is capable of adapting to the specific characteristics of these data sets.

Linear models that operate outside their parameter space require specialized optimization techniques to ensure effectiveness. When working with infinite datasets, model parameters necessarily exist within a finite-dimensional space, posing a problem that needs to be addressed. A common approach involves using stochastic gradient descent to find the optimal parameters, but this method is not time-efficient and can produce suboptimal results when time is a key variable. A recent solution called Time-Tactran, which leverages the strengths of tensor transformation to accelerate and optimize linear model performance for time-series data, has been discovered. By processing data through a series of transformations that exploit its infinite-dimensional nature, Time-Tactran can achieve a 3-dimensional representation of the data and, as a result, delivers enhanced performance and a significant reduction in computing resources. The positive impact of this method on linear model performance, particularly when dealing with time-dependent variables of infinite scope, has been clearly demonstrated through the inclusion of multiple experimental examples.

As demand response and energy storage become more prevalent, understanding the dynamics of forecasts made by individual actors in low-carbon energy systems is crucial for effective policy-making. We examine the principles of risk-averse energy management using storage, demonstrating how risk aversion fundamentally changes the distribution of forecasts, particularly by inducing skewness in predicted prices and supplies. We show how storage risks and rewards become asymmetric, with closer examination revealing the presence of risk-seeking behavior in certain scenarios. Utilizing loss functions from economics, we interpret storage's asymmetric risks through the lens of storage users' attitudes towards risk, with implications for how policies, such as price forecasts and renewable energy curtailment, are designed and managed. We highlight the limitations of current storage modeling, including the exclusion of forecasting errors and the possibility of biased risk estimates, with possible solutions proposed, including the use of advanced simulation methods for modeling risks incurred by individual actors in energy systems.

Using a reduced gravity model with a highly eccentric solar orbit, we simulated the Martian atmosphere's circulation patterns over a 20-Solar-day period. This model included a range of scales, from the global to the storm level, and revealed striking resemblances with Earth's baroclinic storms. We observed the development of mid-latitude storms on the modelled Mars, with characteristics similar to those found on Earth, such as the formation of wavy jet streams, the growth of storms at their edges, and the creation of a permanent polar hood. A comparative study with Earth's atmosphere showed that the imitations of baroclinic behaviour on Mars were very similar, with the exception of some key differences, notably the much longer duration of its storms.

Machine learning models often require massive datasets for training, making acquisition of representative sample data a significant obstacle in classification tasks. To efficiently scale model training, active learning is a promising strategy, which involves selecting the most informative samples from a large pool for labeling. Once labeled, these samples are used to train the model, then it is deployed to classify all unabeled data points. Traditional active learning algorithms generally perform well on small benchmark datasets; however, their effectiveness declines substantially when applied to large datasets like ImageNet. In response to this challenge, we propose a novel active learning strategy that adapts to large datasets by focusing on reducing dataset size through active selection and concurrent transfer learning. In comparison to existing methods, our proposed strategy yields a significantly larger margin of accuracy when classifying a smaller subset of data. When applied to large datasets like ImageNet, our method demonstrates superior performance, with an achieved accuracy of 69.5% compared to 57.2% achieved by the conventional approach.

Achieving precise control over two-qubit operations in quantum processors requires effectively manipulating coupled spin segments through various methods, such as NMR or solid-state systems. Our study focuses on a specific approach, where a single phosphorus atom is combined with nearby silicon vacancies in silicon to serve as a two-qubit unit. By utilizing a robust theoretical framework that accounts for both valley and spin dynamics in N-V centers, we demonstrate the capability to execute a range of two-qubit logic operations with high precision. The results show that by optimizing the position of the donor relative to the N-V center, both the coupling strength and noise from unwanted qubit interactions can be significantly reduced, enabling the execution of two-qubit gate operations for up to 10 microseconds without decoherence. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability to execute a 4-qubit algorithm using two coupled qubits, meeting the prerequisites for scalable quantum computing.

Researchers have long sought to investigate the behavior of electrons in strong magnetic fields within semiconductor microstructures, specifically those near the zero Landau level, which has been notoriously challenging to study due to its extremely short duration. In this study, we observe a widespread phenomenon of electric resistance fluctuations in macroscopic samples of cadmium telluride in the presence of a high magnetic field, particularly within the range of Landau levels closest to each other. By examining the position of the zero Landau level in relation to its neighboring levels through applied electric fields, we uncover a surprising result - a clear shift in the resistance peaks in synchronization with the zero Landau level, despite being confined to a very narrow energy range. Our findings are supported by an intuitive theory based on scattering between two closely adjacent Landau levels, which generates edge currents that can be either in-phase or out-of-phase with each other, ultimately giving rise to resistance oscillations as a result of their scattering. By accurately accounting for the unique characteristics of quantum wells, we successfully explain the recent discovery of a broader resistance envelope, which displays a non-uniform pattern of minima and maxima in the zero Landau level region.

A key challenge in dynamic TDD systems is allocating power and scheduling, which significantly affects data transfer rates. To address this challenge, we develop a novel framework that converts single-band TDD problems into multiple-band TDD ones, enabling the efficient use of both time and frequency resources. Within this framework, we formulate a co-primary and a secondary band allocation problem to minimize the total time required for data transfer, subject to constraints on uplink and downlink transmission times and variable channel coefficients. To solve this non-convex problem, we propose a distributed algorithm that includes a scheduling sub-algorithm and a co-primary allocation sub-algorithm, both of which are shown to converge to the optimal solution. Additionally, we provide a comparable solution for the co-primary band allocation problem that includes a simplified scheduling sub-algorithm and a proportional fair scheduling sub-algorithm, both of which ensure that the time required for data transfer is within the desired limit. To evaluate the performance of the proposed solution, we conduct simulations that demonstrate a significant improvement in data transfer rates and a reduction in the required time, with a 5.67 times increase in the throughput per unit time in a two-band TDD system.

In this study, Hamiltonian Neural Networks are used to model the dynamics of multiple systems that include the well-known MNIST dataset for classification and a mechanical oscillator for demonstrating fundamental principles. A comparison is made between the performance of a Hamiltonian Neural Network and an LSTM-based meta-learner when learning a simple physical law, with results showing a higher accuracy when using HNNs. An important observation made is that when generalizing to new parameters, the Hamiltonian Neural Network retains its precision, in contrast to the LSTM-based meta-learner which experiences a decline in performance. A key aspect of the Hamiltonian Neural Network is its adherence to the fundamental physical principles of conservation of energy. This property is ensured through the use of a specific training objective that enforces the protection of important physical attributes such as symmetries and conservation laws. The associated costs and benefits of using this training objective are also explored in the project.

In a collaborative learning framework, multiple agents work together to achieve a common goal, and the success of this approach depends heavily on the reliability of cooperation among the agents. Unfortunately, some agents might deliberately provide inaccurate data to gain an unfair advantage, which could compromise the effectiveness of the network. This research introduces a novel, decentralized cooperative learning system where agents can appraise each other's credibility and cooperate only with trusted parties. Each agent maintains a local reputation system and makes strategic decisions about cooperation and data sharing based on past experiences. This approach prevents uncooperative agents from gaining an unfair advantage and ensures that the network remains robust in the presence of malicious nodes. The proposed system was tested in a simulated environment, and the results showed significant improvements in the accuracy of machine learning models and the trust score of reputable agents when compared to traditional approaches.

A recently introduced polynomial invariant from 2019, specifically $J_n^T$, was initially proposed as a distinguished polynomial invariant for a specific class of links - those with a particular property of having n-crossings that also satisfy a condition of being m-component alternating links. A significant discovery was made in 2022, revealing that $J_n^T$ actually generates polynomial invariants for links characterized by their n-crossings. This paper aims to enhance earlier work by demonstrating that $J_n^T$ can be expressed as a combination of the Jones polynomial and another polynomial invariant known as the Kauffman polynomial under the constraint of having 1 component and no alternating properties. Furthermore, it will be proven that $J_n^T$ lacks the ability to distinguish between links of 2 components and those of 1 component.

Deep learning models for natural language processing have a problem: they perform incredibly well on the data they were trained on, but struggle with new data. One solution to this limitation is data augmentation, the practice of creating more training data by transforming existing information in a way that adds diversity without degradation. While effective, the effectiveness of data augmentation relies heavily on the specific method employed and the underlying NLP task being performed. 

This book provides a comprehensive overview of the latest data augmentation techniques for natural language processing, covering both traditional methods and more modern deep learning-based approaches. Beginning with an examination of the underlying mechanics driving the success of data augmentation, the book then delves into a detailed analysis of the most effective techniques for various text preprocessing tasks, such as tokenizing, normalizing, and modifying textual data. 

Augmentation techniques that leverage generative models to produce more raw text data are also explored in depth, along with an examination of the most successful methods for augmenting semantic structures, particularly those related to language tasks like machine translation and dialogue. The book also examines the critical issue of selecting the most effective data augmentation strategies for various deep learning models, along with a detailed analysis of the most successful applications and a look at the future of data augmentation in NLP.

The theory of complex representations for certain special functions, such as the Gamma function, can be understood through the study of their integral definitions along the Hankel path. This paper begins with a detailed examination of the Gamma function's representation along the Hankel path, followed by an expansion of its associated kernel through a Toeplitz operator decomposition. Subsequent sections generalize these concepts to the M\"obius form of the Euler Gamma function and the generalized Gamma function, represented along the Hankel path. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates how these representations can be re-expressed as the action of a Toeplitz operator on a specific set of functions, parameterized by the points on the Hankel path.

Recent top quark production measurements at the Large Hadron Collider are compared to different theoretical predictions from the Standard Model, particularly focusing on the top-antitop quark pair production cross section. The data cross section sections are compared to various theoretical estimates in three scenarios: with all corrections up to order istructure, with leading-order plus next-to-leading order corrections, and with next-to-next-to-leading order predictions. The comparison shows that the measured cross section aligns with the predicted values from the Standard Model, exhibiting consistency at a $2\sigma$ significance level. The measured cross section also narrows down the range of possible strong coupling constants, ultimately leading to a more precise determination of $\alpha_S$ when combined with other measurements.

In the current scenario where databases often lack complete information, it is essential to develop methods that can accurately predict missing data. This study presents a framework that combines multi-task learning and convolutional neural networks to enhance data precision in the presence of partial database entries. Unlike conventional approaches, this framework's database is represented as a set of image patterns where each feature corresponds to a column in the database table. By using CNN, the framework predicts unseen data with high accuracy, even when database entries are very limited. Experimental results show that the proposed method delivers superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in the absence of extensive database contents.

This work delves into the computational challenges of privacy loss estimation in differentially private machine learning, particularly within graph-based structures such as neural networks with interconnected nodes. Contrary to standard assumptions of independent data points, the interconnections significantly entangle the privacy losses, leading to a complex optimization problem with multiple optima and a lack of a single, universally optimal solution. The problem is further compounded by the need to account for the target model's predictive purposes, where the optimal solution may depend on the specific application. The paper's key contributions involve introducing a novel definition of a privacy loss factor that captures the collective impact of interconnections and sparse regression algorithms, and subsequently developing an efficient method for computing a lower-bound on privacy losses, along with an empirical study highlighting the method's effectiveness within neural network settings. The study demonstrates that the proposed approach can be particularly beneficial when access to the training dataset is available, by accelerating the computation of lower-bounds by several orders of magnitude while improving the accuracy of estimates by several factors of magnitude compared to current methods.

The Euclid mission's extensive astronomical and cosmological data sets will provide significant benefits for various astronomical research areas including the study of local groups of galaxies, the evolution of stars in the Milky Way, and the dynamics of cosmological populations over vast distances and periods of time. By examining these data, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of fundamental questions such as: How have galaxies and celestial objects, including planets and brown dwarfs, evolved and developed over time? What are the properties and distribution of dark matter and dark energy? To achieve these scientific goals, advanced data analysis will be applied to the vast amounts of data collected by the Euclid mission, with a focus on addressing the significant computational challenges involved.

Developing efficient numerical methods to accurately capture quantum correlations in many-body systems is a pressing issue. The hydrodynamic approach, based on coarse-graining local densities, offers a promising solution by bypassing the computational expenses associated with particle-level simulations. However, the appearance of quantum correlations necessitates a more refined treatment, as they can become lost during the averaging process in a hydrodynamic context. In this work, we introduce a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic method for implementing quantum noise reduction, specifically designed to preserve the effects of quantum correlations. By deviating from a deterministic evolution, the method allows for an enhanced capture of non-equilibrium quantum correlations, as demonstrated through comparisons with other methods using two exemplary models: the Jaynes-Cummings circuit and the driven Jaynes-Cummings system. Our findings reveal that this approach outperforms traditional hydrodynamic methods and other alternatives, such as the quadratic drift method and the Lindblad master equation, especially in the regime where quantum correlations are strongly entangled with fluctuations in the environment. The proposed method's effectiveness is shown to be a critical factor in achieving a correct simulation of quantum correlations within quantum optomechanical systems, both in the steady-state and under periodic driving conditions.

We investigate the rare events of a renewal process whose inter-arrival times are determined by a random matrix, specifically the syntactic matrix of a finite state irreducible and aperiodic Markov process.  This renewal theory is closely tied to the study of the quenched large deviation principle (LDP) for letter sequences under a Markovian dynamics.  Our main achievement is to establish both the tail exponent of the renewal process's rare events and the quenched LDP for letter sequences at the same optimal growth rate, $\lambda_c$.  This demonstrates that the optimal quenched LDP rate function vanishes exactly when the tail exponent of the renewal process does not take a jump, which we prove occurs whenever the random matrix model exhibits a phase transition does not include the parisi phase transition.  The required background on the parisi phase transition is reviewed in the paper's introduction.  Our results rely on interpreting the renewal process through the lens of the empirical process on the set of probability measures on the alphabet of letter sequences.  This interpretation enables us to apply the full force of the central limit theorem for empirical processes, which in turn allows us to establish the desired connection between the tail exponent of the renewal process and the quenched LDP for letter sequences. If a map f from a 2-connected manifold M to a 1-connected manifold N is relatively 1-homotopic and certain conditions regarding its degree are met, we demonstrate that it is 1-homotopic to a map whose image under the universal covering projection is 1-homotopic to a constant map. If the second homotopy group of N is trivial except for degree, we show that the space of relatively 1-homotopic maps from M to N is path-connected.

Recent studies on 64Ni utilizing the RIBF at RIKEN with the MINOS detector revealed a highly excited state spectrum following inelastic scattering of a beam of 64Ni. The unique access to this previously unexplored energy range allows for comparisons with theoretical models of the nucleus. By comparing with the EMY nuclear shell model, discrepancies were found in the low-lying energy levels of 64Ni, specifically in the magnitude of the two-body M1 interaction. This rarefied nucleus, with a well-defined neutron gap at N=40, exhibits extensive clustering properties. The absence of pairing in the middle layers of the nucleus is believed to contribute significantly to the M1 strengths. The distinct lack of the neutron proton interaction in the middle layers of the nucleus is referred to as the N=40 shield. Theoretical calculations utilizing the GCM Wignerian approach, with the CD-Bonn potential as input, are also compared to the data. These calculations, utilizing a generated set of basis states that include both Nilsson configurations and clustering, provide a better explanation of the M1 transition strengths. J-K-fold cross-validation is an untested method that involves dividing a dataset into K non-overlapping subsets of approximately equal size, then randomly selecting J subsets to train and evaluate a model, before moving on to a new random selection of J subsets for the next iteration. This process continues until the model has been evaluated against all possible combinations of K non-overlapping subsets of size J, providing a performance estimate that is claimed to offer improved stability compared to standard K-fold cross-validation. However, an examination of the underlying mechanics of J-K-fold cross-validation reveals that it actually leads to significantly decreased stability of performance estimates, as well as increased computational costs when compared to standard K-fold cross-validation. This is particularly true when working with large datasets. A new approach called progressive K-fold cross-validation is also discussed, which involves dividing a dataset into K non-overlapping subsets of approximately equal size, then randomly selecting one subset to train and evaluate a model, before moving on to a new random selection of a different subset for the next iteration. This process continues until the model has been evaluated against all possible single subsets, after which a new random selection of K non-overlapping subsets is created and the process repeats itself. This method is found to provide significantly improved stability of performance estimates compared to standard K-fold cross-validation, while also offering decreased computational costs when compared to J-K-fold cross-validation.

In order to facilitate the performance of lightweight student networks compared to deep teacher networks, Teacher-Student architectures typically allocate more parameters to teachers. However, this distribution often hinders the development of efficient neural networks, particularly for mobile applications. This paper introduces a novel negative sampling T-Student (NS-TS) loss function that enables a lightweight student to learn from a standard neural network teacher without the need for allocated parameters. Unlike conventional T-Student methods, the proposed NS-TS approach does not assign more parameters to the teacher network. Instead, it uses randomly selected negative samples to train the student, thereby reducing computational costs. This method also facilitates the exploration of lightweight student architectures without the constraint of allocated parameters in the teacher. Experimental evaluations conducted on multiple datasets and network architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed NS-TS method in enhancing the performance of lightweight student networks compared to conventional T-Student methods.

Bayesian inference and optimization are challenging when working with large dynamic systems due to the rapid growth of their representation sizes. Traditional methods for efficient computation, such as Variable Elimination and Distributed Enumeration, are often hampered by the need for frequent variable eliminations and domain intersections across their components. A more efficient algorithm, Bucket Elimination, leverages a coarse-grained partition of the system's variables, enabling a more localized approach to computation, but with the requirement of an exact tree underlying its implementation. When an exact tree is unavailable, a suboptimal solution can be found through a more general Bucket Elimination framework, although one that requires more comparisons. This paper presents a new Bucket Elimination scheme that exploits the structure of dynamic systems to the benefit of both inference and optimization tasks, outperforming the existing approaches by means of a more streamlined comparison matrix and a more localized computation. The newly proposed algorithm, which we call Fast Bucket Elimination, is shown to be a more efficient solution method for the task of finding the most likely explanation in a dynamic system compared to current methods, as demonstrated through example applications and computational experiments.

At high intensities, the interaction between matter and light becomes mutually influential, where the absorption of light by particles isn't just followed by their emission, but also affects the way light is scattered and absorbed in return. This two-way interaction results in a shift in frequency of absorbed light, which we analyzed using a quantum-electrodynamical approach in both free and confined environments. When light is freely present, a peculiar lineshape emerges due to the interplay between saturation and the shift in frequency, taking on a distinctive form that differs from both Lorentzian and Doppler broadening. This specific lineshape can be observed through high-frequency oscillations in the spectrum of a highly saturated absorption process, particularly notable in microwave cavities where a single photon occupies multiple energy levels, causing a big change in how the particle moves back and forth under light influence, which we simulated using both analytical and numerical methods, also discussing the possibility of its direct detection through sensitive microwave absorption in a setup with a cavity.

Recent studies have introduced the concepts of frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming, resulting in the discovery of distinct critical behaviors. Notably, it has been observed that the exponents characterizing the transitions between these states of matter are non-universal and distinguishable from one another. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework based on the constraints of mechanical equilibrium to compare these states and their associated critical properties. By applying the Lindemann criterion to jamming, we were able to map the isotropic jamming transition line on the temperature-pressure plane of a harmonic theory of discrete elasticity. Through this mapping, we were able to determine the pressure exponent of the isotropic jamming transition, which we found to be (1/2) in the harmonic theory of discrete elasticity. In addition, we were able to demonstrate the existence of the frictionless shear jamming state and the possibility of achieving it through the application of pressure in the harmonic theory of discrete elasticity. We were also able to distinguish the characteristics of frictionless shear jamming from those of frictionless isotropic jamming by investigating the stability of the jammed state to shear transformations. Notably, we found that the pressure exponent of the frictionless shear jamming transition is (1/3) in the harmonic theory of discrete elasticity.

This research examines the centralizer $Z(n)^{sl_2}$ within the Borel subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{gl}_n$, focusing on its composition factors when acted upon by the symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_n$. The associated Hilbert-Poincaré series is expressed as a linear combination of basic harmonic polynomials, derived from a detailed analysis of the underlying geometry. A key aspect explored involves the properties of the composition factors, their behavior under the action of the symmetric group, and the associated harmonic polynomials. This work also develops methods for constructing key elements of the centralizer $Z(n)^{sl_2}$, including its composition factors and the harmonic polynomials that form its basis. These methods enable the computation of the Hilbert-Poincaré series for the centralizer $Z(n)^{sl_2}$ for up to $n=6$, and demonstrate how its composition factors mirror a pattern seen in the harmonic polynomials. Furthermore, this research reveals that the properties of the harmonic polynomials can be generalized to the setting of the Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{gl}_{n|n}$, leading to the discovery of new elements within its centralizer $Z(n|n)^{sl_{2|2}}$.

Public sector professionals heavily rely on Web search results for their decision-making, but aren't aware that these searches can be influenced by algorithmic biases. Given the significant impact of Web search on their work, it's essential to consider how algorithmic manipulation affects them, including potential attempts to corrupt election outcomes. To understand the scope of this issue, we conducted an in-depth analysis of Wikipedia edits related to the 2015 UK General Election in order to better comprehend the spread of false information and its influence on search results. Our study reveals how misinformation can spread on Wikipedia, influencing search engine rankings and how efforts to combat this misinformation can sometimes exacerbate the problem. Furthermore, we examine the theoretical limits of which Web searches can be effectively manipulated and explore the policy implications for the management of Wikipedia and the regulation of Web search engines.

A TeV-scale muon collider with several terawatts of peak power and both 1-10 TeV and 10-100 TeV energy ranges could potentially complement a future Higgs or 100 TeV proton collider by offering a broad spectrum of physics capabilities. Within this paradigm, we examine the capabilities of such a muon collider to produce rare particles, such as heavy neutral leptons, light Higgs bosons from scalar sectors, and additional Higgs bosons from weak symmetry breaking. A theoretical framework that incorporates a wide range of physics beyond the Standard Model, based on general effective field theories, is utilized to assess the sensitivity of this collider to these rare phenomena, considering both background-free signature channels and various smearing conditions. Our study reveals that a 1-10 TeV muon collider can produce a significant number of rare events in forward directions, largely unaffected by collimation losses, and that its physics reach compares favorably to that of a 100 TeV proton collider in several cases, highlighting the muon collider's effectiveness in detecting weakly interacting new physics, particularly in the high-energy regime.

The rCASPR sampling technique, which is an enhanced 2D linear sampling method, 
has been developed to meet the complex acquisition needs of modern MRI machines.
In comparison to conventional linear sampling, the rCASPR method achieves a 
significantly smaller point-spread function (PSF) and improved image contrast.
Theoretical analysis and numerical examples demonstrate the improved performance 
of the rCASPR method, showing that it can efficiently reduce data acquisition without 
compromising image quality.
To adapt the rCASPR method to specific MRI machines, a new free-and-open-source 
data reconstruction toolbox called SPARK has been developed, which allows users to 
easily modify sampling patterns to suit their needs and priorities.

The paired-permutation test is a statistical test used to compare the distribution of two populations based on paired data. The test's results can be conducted exactly or approximately using Monte Carlo methods. However, the exact version is now computationally feasible due to a recently developed algorithm, which uses a linear number of computations relative to the data size, and shows superior performance compared to the Monte Carlo method for large datasets. A test framework has been established to demonstrate the effectiveness of the exact algorithm, resulting in a higher success rate when combined with the paired-permutation test. This achievement is particularly significant when working with large datasets from fields like genetics, where accurate statistical analysis is crucial.

This study examines the recent collapse of shipping monopolies, known as shipping cartels, which were widely accepted as providing stability in global shipping markets. Using extensive data from 1993 to 2017 for the three main shipping routes, our analysis reveals the precise time frame in which the cartels broke down and the significant effects this had on shipping prices and quantities. Contrary to conventional wisdom, our findings show that the decline of shipping cartels led to increased price variability and ultimately, lower shipping prices. This, in turn, boosted the quantity of shipping services in demand. Our research discovered that the most notable impact of the cartels' breakdown occurred during the financial crisis of 2008, when the reduction in shipping prices more than compensated for the significant drop in shipping quantities, ultimately minimizing the overall shipping cost for consumers.

We introduce the concept of loom spaces, a generalization of sinuous spaces, and demonstrate that every loom space is linked to a specific type of triangulation. This underlying triangulation serves as a foundation for a more refined classification of loom spaces. Furthermore, we establish that the class of loom spaces mirrors the category of simplicial complexes through a universal mapping property, effectively providing a geometrically explicit representation of simplicial complexes. This connection also enables us to define a variety of geometric invariants for simplicial complexes by directly borrowing concepts from the loom space framework.

The proliferation of stock data across various platforms has given rise to a vast amount of technical insights being shared among investors. As a result, it is now possible to automate the analysis of these insights with machine learning. However, understanding the fundamental nature of stock data prediction models is crucial before applying such approaches. In this explanation-based guide, we delve into the basic mechanics of stock prediction models, demonstrating how simple strategies like linear regression and decision trees can be trained to generate accurate predictions. By utilizing a step-by-step example featuring a fake stock exchange, we demonstrate how to utilize scikit-learn to train and test a machine learning model for predicting stock values. Additionally, we examine the use of linear models, decision trees, and neural networks in stock prediction, discussing their respective strengths and limitations. By breaking down the complexities of stock prediction into manageable parts, this guide empowers readers to experiment with machine learning on their own stock data exchanges.

This note provides the conversion formulas from the parameters of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory to those in the Higgs Effective Field Theory when analyzing the double Higgs production process. In doing so, the underlying assumptions of both effective theories are compared, and the relationship between their fundamental components is established. By doing this for the double Higgs decay to bb$\tau^+\tau^-$, we obtain a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics and and a unified interpretation of the results in both frameworks.

The fundamental theory of General Relativity, described using differential geometric concepts, is not particularly suited for the type of analytical expansion techniques commonly employed in Parameterization-Based Methods. The typical approach, where physical parameters are substituted into Einstein's field equations, results in overly complex expressions due to the intermingling of geometric and non-geometric notions. This lack of separation makes it difficult to efficiently compute small-scale perturbations around a given background. The proposed solution, called 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization, avoids this issue by first simplifying the complex expressions and then adding parameters one at a time, effectively decoupling the non-geometric influences. This method allows for the analysis of nonlinear interactions between small-scale perturbations and their surroundings. As an illustration, the 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization approach is applied to a simple cosmological model featuring a constant time-like background with linear gravitational waves. The resulting decoupled expressions reveal intriguing phenomena, such as the possible occurrence of nonlinear growth of waves in empty space.

We investigated the movement of a cylindrical object through a granular medium to gain a deeper understanding of the drag it encounters and the object's associated trajectory. The key aspect we focused on was the influence of a driving mechanism on this movement. By utilizing a precise and controlled driving system, we were able to explore the effects of different speeds on the drag experienced by the object and how it behaves in response to being driven at various speeds, both with and without the presence of inertia. Our observations revealed a surprising phenomenon - the drag the object experiences actually decreases as it moves faster, despite the presence of inertia. This behavior was observed consistently, regardless of the presence of inertia and even when the object was driven at high speeds, where the drag it experiences becomes negligible in comparison to the force driving it. We believe its occurrence is linked to the irregular nature of the granular bed and the way the object moves through it, as demonstrated by the need for high forces to start and stop the object, even when there is little to no movement. Additionally, we observed that the object's movement is irregular and can be either steady or erratic, and that there is a specific range of speeds in which the object will become stuck, only to suddenly start moving again, even if the force driving it remains the same. We have proposed a possible explanation for this behavior, one that is based on the irregular nature of the bed and the way the object interacts with it, as well as the need for high forces to start and

This study examines the momenta at which the triangular and elliptic flow patterns peak in a fixed energy scale. Our findings indicate a similar transverse momentum dependence for triangular and elliptic flow in mid-scale momenta. However, in higher momenta, the triangular flow peaks more sharply than the elliptic flow, which can be explained by the non-linear response to initial conditions and the triangular flow's stronger connection to long-wavelength correlations. Our research discovered that the triangular and elliptic flow curves could be made indistinguishable from each other in the same fixed energy scale when accounting for differences in particle production rates. The proportion of charged particles participating in flow patterns is greater for triangular than for elliptic flow, as seen in our study of mid-scale momenta featuring a wide range of particle types. This is particularly evident in the polar angle distribution of Z bosons, which reveal a significant triangular flow signal in central collisions, in contrast to elliptic flow, seen in Z boson collisions with lower energies. Our research further demonstrates that the ratio of triangular over elliptic flow exhibits little variation with energy in a fixed energy scale, in both mid-scale momenta featuring a wide range of particle types and in Z bosons within a certain collision energy range.

This paper provides an overview of rare $B$ meson decays involving the emission of leptons, such as electrons or muons, that occur when a $B^0$ or $B^0_s$ meson transforms into a pair of light particles. The discussion centers on the theoretical understanding and potential experimental studies of these rare events at the LHC. Rare $B$ meson decays are characterized by weak interaction forces that bypass the strong force binding the hadrons together, and are often accompanied by the emission of a gluon that can be accounted for through theoretical corrections. The most remarkable of these decays, such as $B^0_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$, are extremely rare, with rates that, when measured through experiments, provide a sensitivity of approximately two orders of magnitude beyond the most elementary particle theories. The discussion highlights the latest experimental measurements from the LHC experiments at CERN, the potential for future discoveries at the luminous LHC, and the theoretical framework underpinning these rare events.

This research introduces a novel FGMRES iteration framework, which enhances the
standard FGMRES method by incorporating a matrix multiplication step within the
iteration. The proposed approach leads to a higher level of accuracy, especially
in cases where the matrix multiplication is computationally efficient compared to
the system of equations being solved. Theoretical analysis of the proposed method
reveals that its convergence rate is comparable to that of the original FGMRES. The
FGMRES modification is then applied to the time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations
in a two-dimensional cavity, using both finite differences and spectral elements
methods for spatial and temporal discretization, respectively. The resulting linear
systems are solved using the proposed FGMRES modification, which demonstrates its
effectiveness in achieving a higher degree of accuracy with a smaller number of
iteration steps. The numerical examples show that the proposed FGMRES method can
lead to a 5 orders of magnitude reduction in the residual when combined with the
$O(10^{-3})$ accuracy level, in comparison to the original FGMRES which may require
a 10 times increase in the number of iteration steps to achieve the same level
of accuracy.

Accurate model-to-data registration is crucial in surgery to guide procedures and minimize risks. However, intraoperative data is often noisy, which hinders the performance of registration techniques, particularly for complex surgeries on critical organs like the liver. In this paper, a novel deep learning-based method is introduced that jointly estimates the deformation field and organ model from noisy intraoperative data with the goal of improving the robustness of registration in challenging surgeries. By pretraining on a large dataset of simulated noisy data, the network is able to withstand significant levels of noise, outperforming conventional registration methods by a significant margin in multiple noise scenarios, according to registration accuracy results obtained through extensive simulation studies. Additionally, the proposed technique is applied to an actual dataset of 20 liver surgery cases, with the findings demonstrating its practical utility. A comparison with a state-of-the-art graph-based method is also presented for comparison purposes.

Establishing a reliable and robust method for estimating optical flow without supervision remains a pressing issue. Self-supervised learning offers a promising solution by eliminating the need for annotated data, but certain challenges like occlusions and scene changes pose significant obstacles for current techniques. In this research, we address these difficulties by introducing a novel method that leverages temporal information to enhance the accuracy of self-supervised optical flow estimation. Rather than utilizing two consecutive frames, our network processes three frames with defined relationship for improved performance. Comprehensive experiments on various datasets reveal that our network surpasses existing self-supervised flow estimation methods and even achieves comparable results to supervised methods on the Middlebury dataset. Additionally, our network demonstrates improved performance on challenging scenes with occlusions and scene changes in the Driving Dataset and the KITTI dataset.

A purpose-built neural network, known as a Spike-Time-Encoded Perceptron (STEP), is introduced, capable of serving as a versatile classifier that outperforms energy-efficient spiking neural networks (SNNs) while minimizing power expenditures. By converting training data into spike times and leveraging a unique, bio-inspired learning process called Spike-Time-Dependent Plasticity, STEP can achieve classification performance on par with traditional artificial neural networks (ANNs). The proposed network is designed to function with intrinsically low power by only consuming energy during spike events, and STEP's compact structure, characterized by a minimal number of layers, further enhances energy efficiency. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through classification tasks on large datasets, including a 28-layer STEP to efficiently classify large datasets like CIFAR-5 and a highly compact 2-layer STEP to efficiently classify a synthetic dataset with 100 classes.

Theoretical studies of strong magnetic fields' effects on quark matter's state equation are presented for spin-polarized strange quark matter. The Dirac form factor and the electromagnetic interactions were taken into consideration using a modified MIT bag model. The interaction between the quark's gluon fields and the electromagnetic field was also examined to ensure the stability of strange quark matter regarding electric charge. The calculation demonstrates that, at high magnetic fields, the quark matter's pressure becomes negative, but this does not affect the mechanism by which electric charge is confined. It is also shown that a state of pure electrical neutrality can be achieved through a mechanism known as the "mezonization" of quark matter. The study further reveals the existence of a critical magnetic field that induces a phase transition from a neutral to a charged state of strange quark matter. The calculation also indicates the existence of two critical densities where the quark matter's pressure turns positive, and a phase transition from strange quark matter to nuclear matter is triggered. The study further reveals that the neutron star's canonical mass can be explained if strange quark matter exists at a density lower than the one required for the pressure to become positive. The study also provides the expression for the neutron star's canonical mass in terms of its radius and the speed of light, and presents numerical solutions for a specific type of star with a radius of 16.8 km.
