A cubic graph is considered even-2-factorable (E2F) if it has factors of 2k and 4k edges, with no common divisor other than 2. Our research reveals that every 2-factorable cubic graph either falls into the even-2-factorable category or has a factor of 6 with a specific type of 3-edge-coloring. This discovery leads to the conclusion that every cubic graph that is a 6-factor has the property of being even-2-factorable. Consequently, our findings address two problems posed by the London Combinatorial Survey and the Belair Survey, respectively.

This paper introduces a novel, efficient system call filtering technique called
Timeloops for applications utilizing interpreted languages such as PHP, Python,
Node.js, and Ruby. Interpreted applications typically rely on virtualized or
privileged environments for security, yet this approach precludes system call
filtering for these apps. In contrast, Timeloops provides a user-friendly,
high-performance way to apply system call filters to interpreted applications.
Underlying the Timeloops system is a custom, lightweight binary format that
allies efficiency with security features. This binary format ensures that system
calls behave as expected and permits the enforcement of fine-grained policies
on system calls. To accommodate the diverse system call interfaces presented
by various operating systems and applications, Timeloops employs a sophisticated
module architecture offering extensive flexibility. In addition to its modular
design, the Timeloops system comprises an efficient loop optimizer that
significantly minimizes the number of system calls made by the application.
Overall, Timeloops yields a notable decrease in execution speed losses, a
performance degradation experienced by applications undergoing system call
verification. In the course of conducting our research, the Timeloops team
discovered multiple notable findings, including the revelation that many
applications overlook key system call functionality or misinterpret API
specifications due to their lack of direct access to source code. To facilitate
wide adoption of the Timeloops system, we open-source it and contribute it to
the public domain.

This study proposes a probabilistic method for predicting the positions of targets that have gone undetected within a network of sensors with limited fields of view. Unlike conventional approaches, this method bypasses the need for continuous scanning of the entire surveillance area by focusing on areas around lead detections. By doing so, the computational load is significantly reduced while still allowing for efficient target tracking. Moreover, this method enables the prediction of potential positions of targets that have been out of sight for an extended period and could potentially re-emerge within the sensor network's field of view.

This study examines the dynamics of a competitive model, specifically the Lotka--Volterra system with consumer--resource interactions, within an infinite boundary population. By establishing a crucial observability inequality for a related PDE system, we demonstrate the existence of a global positive solution when the initial population is confined to a finite region. This approach enables us to manage population growth or decline within any designated time frame, thereby preventing extinction. By leveraging this strategy, we show that any positive initial data, however small, will eventually give rise to a globally defined solution of the underlying PDE system.

We're exploring the underlying rewards behind soccer players' actions, seeking to assign numerical values to their behavior. In doing so, we're creating a framework that allows us to generate synthetic SCENIC datasets, mirroring real-game patterns. By applying this framework to a handful of predefined scenarios, we've discovered intriguing contrasts in reward potential. For instance, committing a foul often yields higher rewards than taking a shot, except when the opponent is close to scoring. Similarly, losing possession by kicking the ball out of bounds is generally more rewarding than shooting, except in certain time-sensitive situations. We've also compared the most rewarding actions in various situations and offer practical takeaways for coaches on how to manage situations effectively.

A common issue in the implementation of time-domain wavefields for Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) arises when trying to handle large models due to the excessive memory requirements for time-domain wavefields, specifically when using the Kirchhoff Integral Method (KIM) or Finite-Difference methods. Another challenge is the need for a large amount of time to compute wavefield extensions, which can be very time-consuming, particularly when using the Finite-Difference method. In order to overcome these limitations, this work leverages the Fast Kirchhoff Synthetic Integral (FKSI) method, which generates synthetic wavefields through the rapid application of a convolution operation between the seismic source and a precomputed set of integral kernels, relying on the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) for an efficient solution. A key advantage of FKSI is its ability to compute wavefield extensions in a matter of seconds, making it suitable even for large-scale models. Additionally, FKSI allows for the implementation of time-domain FWI using the classical iterative BFGS method, which can be challenging with other wavefield formulations. The proposed method is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments on synthetic data and real-field data, for both surface and crosswell acquisitions, using FKSI with the classical iterative BFGS method and producing comparable results to other time-domain FWI implementations.

To examine the effects of random events and spatial distance on the dynamics of two interacting species in a population, an asymmetric noisy voter model is employed as its basic framework. The model, set within a square network of N individuals, allows for the diffusion of opinions between nearby agents and the occasional random change of an individual's own opinion. Due to the absence of symmetry in the model, different outcomes can arise, including the formation of distinct opinion domains, the breakdown of spatial opinion gradients, or the uniform spread of opinions. A comprehensive mathematical study of this model is conducted through the analysis of its stochastic process, where the reduction of a continuous time formulation into a discrete one reveals a nonlinear interplay between the rates of random opinion changes and the formation of opinion boundaries. The subsequent exploration of the reduced model through Monte Carlo simulations and the direct comparison with numerical results reveal the existence of a nonequilibrium phase transition in the model, characterized by the sudden emergence of a rigid opinion gradient in the absence of random events. The associated universality class is identified as that of the Kosterlitz-Thouleses model through the observation of universal scaling laws in the model's nonequilibrium phase transition.

In a 2D Data and Energy Transfer (DED2D) system, a novel time and frequency indexing and encoding technique (TFIET) is proposed to transfer both data and energy to users. This method assigns a unique set of time, frequency, and power indices to each user, enabling simultaneous communication and energy harvesting with minimal interference. A TFIET-based precoder is then used to create low-interference signals for users, facilitating efficient and secure communication. This study explores the optimal time and frequency division to maximize the overall data transfer rate in a 4-user DED2D system, utilizing a TFIET scheme with 4 time slots and 4 frequency subbands, and demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique in a real-world scenario.

The pandemic-driven shift to remote work has significantly impacted the way experiments are set up and conducted. As a result, there is a growing need for automated setups that minimize physical interaction and ensure consistency across repetitions. This paper addresses this emerging challenge by presenting a robotic setup that performs a specific task efficiently and consistently, and it does so in a way that is accessible to others who might be interested in automating similar experiments. By leveraging a relatively affordable and adaptable setup, this solution enables others to automate their own experiments and reproduce the methods used here with ease.

The impact of electrostatic phase plates, specifically their design features 
such as fill-factor and pixel pattern, on electron probe size and current density 
is analyzed using a simulation that accounts for aberration correction. The 
simulation allows for the examination of how different design elements, including 
scan patterns and fill-factors, individualized to accommodate varying sample 
requirements, affect the performance of the electron optic system. It is shown 
that the probe current density and size are directly opposed, making them 
conflicting objectives in electron optic system design. A method to calculate 
the Sharpe ratio is also presented, along with an analysis of how it is affected 
by design variables, particularly in the context of a scanning transmission 
electron microscope (STEM). It is demonstrated that the optimal design of phase 
plates can significantly improve the performance of STEM instruments, with one 
example showing that an increase from a 1 Angstrom probe size to 0.5 Angstrom 
is possible with only a 40-fold decrease in current density, reaching levels 
necessary for electron holography with a 10 kElectron Volts (eV) acceleration 
voltage.

We investigate the orbital stability of solitary waves in a one-dimensional system that consists of two interacting species: a harmonic oscillator and an anharmonic oscillator. By introducing a small anharmonic component to a otherwise pure harmonic oscillator through a coupling term, we examine the effects on the orbital stability of a solitary wave that arises from this interaction. Using a conservation law, we show that the symmetry of the wave's configuration under a shift in its center will be conserved over time, which indicates that the anharmonic component has a negligible impact on the orbital stability of the wave. Additionally, we find that the presence of anharmonicity also results in the emission of waves by the solitary wave, which can be described by a damped harmonic oscillator equation. Based on these findings, we provide a rough estimate of the emission time, which indicates that the anharmonic component's effect on the orbital stability of a solitary wave is very limited, occurring only within a very short distance and over a very brief period of time.

We provide a detailed characterization of the Galois module structure for a particular type of finite non-abelian extension, denoted as K/Q, where the Galois group G = Gal(K/Q) exhibits both wild ramification and the property of being abelian in a substantial subgroup while featuring a non-trivial central element. Our analysis demonstrates that such a context is equivalent to a specific computational problem, solving which yields an intuitive representation of G through a set of generators and defining relations. This problem can be solved by constructing specific polynomial equations whose solutions correspond to the elements of G. A non-abelian extension with wild ramification and a specific local characteristic at a prime p is also investigated in this study.

This letter describes the creation, decay, and possible detection methods of a neutral long-lived particle (NLP) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Due to its varying decay length, the same NLP cannot be searched for using both prompt and long-lived signatures at the same collider. Consequently, at the LHC, a strategy is proposed that simultaneously uses two distinct sets of experiments: those at low momentum scales that can identify long-lived NLP through unusual patterns of missing energy and charged particles, and those at higher momentum scales that can detect prompt NLP through boson pairs. The effectiveness of this strategy is evaluated through simulations of NLP production, followed by decay into $t \bar t$. The potential of this search method is significant, as it can lead to discoveries at existing colliders and future, more powerful ones.

To better grasp the underlying dynamics of language change, it's crucial to consider the role of context in shaping words' meanings. A common approach in NLP models, contextual variance is a fundamental aspect that can influence the interpretation of semantic shifts, but its own evolution over time is rarely examined. In this work, we investigate the historical development of contextual variance for three expressions in British English, utilizing a vast corpus from the internet. Our findings show that the contextual variance surrounding these expressions altered significantly during the observed period, a phenomenon that could be forecast with high accuracy when contextual variance is modeled independently. Our research also reveals that the primary driver of their semantic change is misdirected, according to some previous research, and that accounting for the shift in contextual variance substantially explains previous results on unidirectional semantic change. Moreover, our work highlights the importance of distinguishing contextual variance from other kinds of changes that could be mistaken for semantic evolution.

Researchers have long sought evidence for QCD axion dark matter, which could exist as a heavy, scalar particle. A non-abelian effective field theory for a single, heavy, scalar particle in the infinite component formalism has been developed, allowing for the calculation of ultra-light particle properties, such as elastic scattering cross-sections and decay widths, in a reliable NLO chiral effective field theory. A crucial finding in this study concerns the relationship between the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the infinite component formalism and the background gauge field, which has been resolved by employing the gradient flow method. By utilizing the properties of the eigenvalue distribution of the Dirac operator, it has been determined that the spectrum of the infinite component formalism consists only of positive mass eigenvalues, which significantly narrows the parameter space for ultra-light particle models. This has major implications for dark matter composed of heavy scalar particles, for which the only possible mechanism is decay from a heavy pseudoscalar particle, identified as the QCD axion.

During retinal development, newly generated neurons must navigate through the retina to their appropriate final positions. Prior research suggested that nuclei are randomly dispersed and then guided to their designated locations by the chemoattractive properties of pre-existing retinal cells. Our study reveals a more complex distribution of nuclei across the retina, with distinct patterns of dispersion in different stages of development. By observing the movement of individual nuclei over time, we discovered that they exhibit directed motion, yet their paths are also characterized by sudden, random changes in direction. This behavior is consistent with the idea that nuclei are drawn to specific retinal locations through chemoattractive cues, but are also susceptible to being diverted by random fluctuations of the surrounding retinal cells. As a result of these interactions, the distribution of nuclei appears disorganized, yet they consistently coalesce into specific patterns of dispersion that reflect their future positions within the retina. Our mathematical model demonstrates how the dynamics of nuclear migration are influenced by the distribution of retinal cells and provides predictions that have been confirmed through the analysis of retinal wholemounts from developing zebrafish.

Compressive sensing has numerous applications in image processing, where the goal is to restore high-dimensional data from a small number of measurements. The effectiveness of this method relies heavily on the choice of sensing matrix. Since the mutual coherence of the matrix plays a crucial role in determining the accuracy of reconstruction, research has focused on developing algorithms that minimize mutual coherence while efficiently utilizing the available measurements. Although these efforts have yielded various optimization and learning-based approaches, the question of whether there is an inherent trade-off between mutual coherence and the number of measurements required remains unclear. This work introduces a novel sparse representation-based method that directly minimizes mutual coherence by constructing a matrix from a set of predetermined signals, and demonstrates the efficacy of this approach in compressive reconstruction, phase retrieval, and super-resolution imaging. The results show that this method achieves superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art, and provides robust solutions that are highly robust to the choice of parameters and other image acquisition artifacts.

The spontaneous movement of certain systems, including the motion of solids broken under tension and the spreading of cellular layers, can be influenced by a linear and weak external force. Despite its significance, there is still a lack of understanding in the dimensions we commonly work in (3D and above) how this movement changes over time, especially when there are many small fluctuations present. The general idea that dynamics must change significantly in these dimensions, becoming fundamentally different from those seen in lower dimensions, is supported by numerous examples. In fact, the movement of these systems can be shown to behave differently in the space we commonly occupy, exhibiting scaling characteristics that differ from those predicted by a simplified hydrodynamic model, even when the effects of noise are minimal. The introduction of random fluctuations, however, cause their movement to converge towards the behavior predicted by a simplified hydrodynamic model, despite their initial different scaling characteristics. This phenomenon is referred to as "weak hydrodynamic failure" and its occurrence has now been demonstrated numerically through simulations of a specific model that mimics the behavior of a random, broken solid surface moving downwards due to gravity.

The proliferation of ID cards issued by various organizations, with different naming conventions and varying data formats, poses a significant challenge for automated text extraction techniques. Deep Learning models have shown improved performance in extracting embedded information but rely heavily on large-scale training datasets. In contrast, small-scale datasets benefit more from simple yet effective techniques that leverage Natural Language Processing enhancements. This research introduces an innovative method, Text2Name, which fine-tunes a Name Embedding model to accurately extract card issuers' names and associated information from small ID card datasets. By leveraging Natural Language Processing techniques, Text2Name enhances the efficacy of text extraction on small datasets, achieving a 20-point F1-score improvement without additional training. This research also explores the benefits of Name Embeddings in combining micro-datasets, eliminating the need for explicit Data Fusion techniques. The proposed solution's performance is consistently high across diverse ID card formats, with an overall F1-score of 0.93 in extracting embedded information.

In this research, a broad class of quantum states for bosonic modes is defined as 'driven coherent states', which includes both coherent states and overtones as specific cases. An important condition, state uniqueness, is applied to determine the parameters that define these states in a driven system with a harmonic oscillator. The calculation method demonstrates the utility of this approach in analyzing the dynamics of driven coherent states. The case of a driven harmonic oscillator with a nonlinear response is particularly explored to demonstrate the application of this approach in analyzing the dynamics of driven coherent states.

An extraordinary phenomenon has been observed in a few asteroids within the Earth-Moon system, where accelerated rotation is a common occurrence. Based on data from PanSTARRS1 and other sources, we discovered five asteroids with rapidly rotating periods, ranging from 114 to 240 minutes, and with features indicating they are non-spherical in shape. By examining their brightness variations over time, we found that their rotation speeds are increasing at rates equivalent to several hundred degrees per year. To explain these findings, we consider possible explanations including tidal forces from the Earth or Moon, but find them insufficient to account for the acceleration observed in most cases. Instead, we propose that these asteroids may be experiencing temporary "wobbling" due to the gravitational influence of small satellite objects, such as moonlets, that are causing slight shifts in their rotational velocities. To support this theory, we suggest that future missions observing these asteroids, particularly the Lucas Survey Telescope, can verify the presence of satellite objects orbiting around them by detecting faint eclipses in their light curves.

We investigate groups acting on the interior of a compact surface without fixed points, focusing on subgroups of surface groups that act freely outside a system of horoballs with convex rims. Our primary objectives are to determine under what conditions these subgroups exhibit transient behavior and to establish that they possess compact fundamental domains within the surface's interior. Our approach is guided by the fundamentals of hyperbolic geometry and dynamical systems, and we establish key results concerning the relationship between these subgroups' actions and their geometric properties. Furthermore, we establish that they satisfy specific growth properties and form a class of groups we term "thinly cocompact," which includes well-known examples such as outer planetary groups and many subgroups derived from them.

In the case of rational functions defined within a finite field, the algorithm demonstrates nearly optimal computational complexity for both continuity decision and rational function reconstruction tasks.

Machine learning models, specifically neuromorphic networks, have been successfully applied to predict the behavior of complex dynamical systems by capturing their underlying patterns. Real-world systems, whether biological, technological or environmental, frequently exist on multiple timescales and exist in various dynamic states, posing a significant challenge for their characterization. We demonstrate how a simple reservoir computing framework can be effective in capturing the essential characteristics of highly intricate systems with distinct time scales and multiple coexisting dynamic states, even in scenarios where only limited training data are available. Our study utilizes a bunse-Ostrum transformation of a chaotic laser system to demonstrate the accuracy of this method, showing that it can generate highly accurate predictions for up to 200 times its own generation time, a performance that exceeds comparable recent work.

This study explores the method for determining the set of states that can be reached from an initial state within a specific time frame during the course of a dynamic process. The aim is to establish the reachability of a state set over time in relation to a system that follows a particular flow of states. The method involves solving two interconnected issues: state transition prediction and state set approximation. The former involves using numerical methods to forecast the path the system will take, while the latter, an iterative process, is comparable to performing castings of state sets through the application of operators derived from the system's dynamics. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of this method by creating a reachable state set computation framework for a specific type of dynamic system. The resulting framework has the capability to handle complex systems with multiple states and outputs, as well as providing the means to account for various constraints that may apply. The study also presents computational results obtained using the method, in addition to examining the impact of feedback control on reachable state sets over time.

Our investigation into the underlying principles of animacy categorization across various domains yields two primary factors: visual categorizability and agency. These elements exist on their own spectrums, unrelated to each other, and together form a cumulative animacy scale that mirrors human perception. Our findings demonstrate that the animacy continuum is intricate and multifaceted, refusing a singular explanation and instead requiring a nuanced, multi-faceted approach. By understanding the animacy continuum through the lens of visual categorizability and agency, researchers and practitioners are equipped with a more precise, empirically supported framework for analyzing the complex animacy dimension that influences human judgment and categorization processes.

We provide a lower estimate for the number of pairs of zeros from an orthonormal basis of automorphic L-functions with fixed broad resonance eliminating narrow zeros, within a specified height parameter D, as the height D increases arbitrarily. This estimate shows that an unbounded number of pairs of zeros can repel each other strongly in an arbitrarily large region of the complex plane, with the rate of this strong repelling phenomenon occurring at a rate of at least a polynomial of degree 1+epsilon in the height variable, as the height increases arbitrarily. This result implies the nonexistence of narrow Landau-Siegel zeros in an arbitrarily large region of the complex plane, with a rate of at least a polynomial of degree 2+epsilon in the height variable, as the height increases arbitrarily. Our previous work demonstrated the nonexistence of narrow Landau-Siegel zeros in a fixed region of the complex plane, with a polynomial degree of at least 2. This achievement is a significant improvement upon our former estimate, a degree of at least 1, which was derived in a past research publication.

We have created an formal logical framework known as Quantum Relational Hoare Logic (QRHL), which serves as a fundamental theory for the verification of properties concerning input-output relationships in programs, taking into consideration their capacity for retrieval and manipulation of data with both classical and quantum components.

This study examines the impact of large-scale transmission events in isolated settings, such as meeting rooms, using a super-spreader model integrated with the standard susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) dynamics. We compare the effectiveness of various models, including a simple Poisson distribution, incorporating exponential and power-law distribution scenarios, and present analytical solutions for the integrated model. We further investigate the impact of these distribution-driven processes on infection dynamics, presenting numerical results for different closure scenarios. Our analysis highlights the critical influence of primary transmission events on epidemic spread and offers quantitative insights into the mechanisms underlying the acceleration of epidemics in enclosed spaces. We demonstrate that the integrated model accurately captures increased transmission risks during super-spreader events and provides actionable guidance for public health strategies in critical settings, such as conference venues, transportation hubs, and military bases.
We provide a new proof that codiskcyclicity of an operator is equivalent to the property of having a $C_0$-semigroup whose generators' adjoinment operators are all invertible.

This study introduces a novel approach to estimating a region's magnetic fill fraction, which is a new parameter that can be used to correct models of a region's vector magnetic field. Researchers can use existing vector magnetic field models, specifically those in the Line-of-Sight component, to calculate the fill fraction without additional data. This method involves creating local snapshots of plasma and magnetic field properties at specific points within a region, and it has been effective in identifying areas with incomplete data, missing magnetic field components, or both. Studies have demonstrated that explicitly considering fill fraction can significantly improve the accuracy of model assessments, especially when there is incomplete data. This approach is particularly useful when predicting the strength of magnetic field lines, calculating free magnetic energy, or identifying regions with strong magnetic field lines.

A novel neural network architecture, specifically designed for efficient Monte Carlo simulations through complex-valued affine coupling layers, has been introduced. This new model's efficient sampling capability is shown to outperform a state-of-the-art real-valued neural network working in tandem with the Euler method, which is considered a high-performance simulation tool within a confined experimental framework. A complex-valued neural network implementing the Euler method to sample a fractional Brownian surface has been trained and its performance evaluated under various simulation settings.

We examine the impact of a recognizable morphism on topological entropy within the context of subshifts. A recognizable morphism generally increases topological entropy except in instances where the image under the morphism corresponds to a subshift with zero topological entropy or when the image is invariant under a given irreducible matrix, in which case the topological entropies remain equal.

To mitigate the challenges of low-data performance in language models, we introduce the ReCross framework, which refines the performance of models through counterfactual optimization on unlabeled data. By leveraging the counterfactual targets generated from high-quality labeled data, we facilitate model improvement without compromising its original capabilities. In the case of a single poorly performing model, we enhance its effectiveness through counterfactual loss calculation. When comparing two underperforming models, we counterfactualize the target for one of them to generate more accurate, contrasting predictions. To achieve this, we draw upon the pairwise ranking information from their respective training datasets. We evaluate the ReCross framework on multiple datasets, demonstrating its superiority over conventional model ensemble techniques.

Machine learning models are frequently enhanced through hyperparameter optimization, but this process is complicated by the need to protect sensitive information contained within private datasets. This limitation renders many efficient, high-performance optimization techniques, such as the grid search method, unusable because they require access to the entire dataset during the optimization process. In contrast, single-point methods that iterate towards the optimal solution by making repeated use of the dataset can be employed, but they tend to converge at a slow rate, resulting in extensive computation time, especially for large-scale hyperparameter spaces. In response to this challenge, we propose a novel efficient single-point optimization algorithm known as the Hyperparameter Optimization via Iteration Elimination (HOIE) framework, which leverages the properties of gradient-based optimization to accelerate the hyperparameter tuning process by excluding unnecessary iterations. By further integrating the HOIE framework with a customized stochastic gradient descent method, we significantly boost the algorithm's performance, as demonstrated by our comparative evaluation using real-world datasets and large-scale synthetic data. These results show that the HOIE framework yields a superior solution at a fraction of the computational cost compared to widely employed single-point optimization algorithms.

An earlier result stating that the number of spheres in a right-angled 2-dimensional wedge is at most $|\Delta|$ has been incorrectly attributed to Michael Davis, and its actual proof follows from a more general estimate involving Coxeter groups, stating that the number of spheres in a 2-dimensional wedge is no greater than the size of any generating set for the associated Coxeter group, and can be equal when the associated Coxeter group has a specific property called being of type F.

The study of chemical elements, specifically light and moderate elements, in chemically distinctive stars through spectroscopy is a powerful tool for uncovering their formation histories. By comparing star spectra to synthetic spectra from vast libraries of stellar models, the composition of individual stars can be determined with high precision, bypassing the need for complex data interpretation through machine learning techniques. A previously developed code, LEAST, is used to automate this process by matching star spectra to the smallest possible set of synthetic spectra from pre-existing model libraries, ensuring consistency in elemental analysis across different models. By analyzing the residual abundances left unexplained by the best-matching models, the code identifies stars with distinctive chemical signatures and provides a record of their individual residual abundance patterns. This approach enables a novel application of abundance residuals to distinguish between different stellar populations and helps resolve the complex histories of stars and their clusters. By comparing abundance residuals directly with the fundamental parameters of the models, LEAST can reproduce the intricate patterns of chemically distinctive stars and accurately decompose their chemical composition into elements with unique spectral features and elements without unique spectral features. This code can be a valuable asset for enhancing the understanding of chemically normal stars and their clusters by exploring the residual abundance patterns that are a direct outcome of its application.

We propose a novel spatio-temporal modeling approach that examines the spread of misinformation across China based on satellite imagery and mobile device data. Our model explores the impact of geographic and temporal factors on the growth and decline of these rumors. By applying peak and attenuation functions, we uncover fascinating insights into the dynamics of misinformation spread. We further leverage the predictive capabilities of our model to conduct policy simulations, such as assessing the effectiveness of removing rumors in specific areas or delaying their dissemination. Our results reveal that certain geographic regions and time periods are more susceptible to the spread of misinformation. We also discover that removing rumors in popular urban centers can significantly reduce peak growth, whereas delaying their dissemination can alter the peak timing with varying regional results. Our research demonstrates the value of telecommunication data in modeling misinformation dynamics and the potential benefits of precision policies in managing their impact.

We conducted a survey for planetary nebulae (PNe) within the Fornax cluster using the VLT/IFU and the 2.5m telescope at the Carajás Observatory in Brazil. This study led to the detection of 247 PNe within the cluster, bringing the total number of detected objects to 434, and allowing for a detailed analysis of the cluster's distance. We created a luminosity function for each sub-cluster based on the brightness distribution of the PNe, and calculated their distances as 19.62 kpc (±0.45 kpc) and 19.53 kpc (±0.43 kpc) for the central and outer regions respectively. The average distance for the entire cluster was then determined as 19.575 kpc (±0.305 kpc) based on the cumulative distribution function of the luminosity function. This value is more precise than previous estimates obtained from globular clusters and RR Lyrae stars, and confirms the earlier suggestion that the Fornax cluster may be part of the Local Group's central bulge.

Recent years have seen a surge in high-performance dynamical modeling using
large datasets, leading to an increase in computational demands. While
accelerated numerical libraries, such as NumPy and SciPy, provide high
performance computations for small to medium-sized datasets, they fall short
for large-scale data, prompting the need for a new approach. In an effort
to bridge this gap, we present LifeStream, an interactive high-performance
numerical library that can be easily integrated into existing data processing
pipelines. LifeStream is designed to handle large datasets of common science
types and features dynamic streaming computation, enabling it to achieve
speed-ups of up to 5x and memory reductions of up to 10x in comparison to
hand-optimized libraries like NumPy and SciPy. We further demonstrate LifeStream's
efficiency through real-world applications, including a 4x performance boost
and a 20x memory savings when processing a 10 GB dataset in just over half a
second.

We provide a precise definition of a Bertrand curve in three-dimensional Euclidean space and a two-dimensional sphere, demonstrating that a curve possesses this property if it has a distinct companion curve with a constant reciprocal curvature. We also examine the characteristics of a Darboux Berbtrand partner curve in these spaces, presenting their fundamental properties and examples.

We analyze the behavior of neural networks when their loss function misaligns with their training objective, considering a range of loss functions, including popular options like Cross-Entropy and Mean Squared Error. By exploring how loss function alignment affects performance, we aim to provide a framework for understanding how networks adapt to mismatched losses and how this adaptation relates to loss alignment. Through in-depth analysis of network responses to loss mismatch, we identify three primary adaptations: degradation, mode mixing, and mode separation. Each is characterized by a distinct response to loss change, governed by network bias, and we demonstrate how network bias influences the outcome of performance changes. Furthermore, we demonstrate how loss alignment impacts the network's ability to generalize, discovering a trade-off between performance on original and new data. Through synthetic experiments and an exploration of existing data, we show that networks often achieve high performance on originally labeled data, even when the loss function is changed to a less effective one, but at the cost of poor generalization, manifesting as a failure to adapt to new, similar data. By manipulating loss function hyperparameters, we induce a network to generalize better, demonstrating the potential to enhance a network's ability to generalize through careful loss function selection.

This study presents a comprehensive thermodynamic framework that accounts for the interplay between chemical and diffusion processes in polymer materials undergoing strain-induced crystallization. By applying the principles of nonequilibrium thermodynamics, non-Newtonian fluid mechanics, and crystal plasticity theory, a hierarchically structured model is developed to predict the morphological and thermal evolution of polymers during crystallization, driven by mechanical stress and temperature differences. By introducing the concept of internal variables and using the GENERIC framework to ensure satisfaction of second law of thermodynamics, the governing equations are reduced to a system of nonlinear partial differential equations that can be numerically solved using a Galerkin method. To facilitate efficient computation, a multiresolution entropy-stable numerical method is employed to solve the equations, and the accuracy of the model is validated through comparisons with experimental data. By applying this model to a range of polymer materials subjected to varying loading conditions and temperature gradients, the results reveal the formation of crystals, the associated thermal responses, and the material degradation, providing a comprehensive understanding of the physical phenomena governing polymer crystallization.

The relationship between the Fermi surface topology and magnetic susceptibility in superconducting materials is governed by the Feynman diagram shown in figure 1, where the gray shapes represent contours of the energy vs. momentum that are constant for a particular wavevector. This diagram shows that the derivative of the free energy with respect to a small magnetic field is equal to the sum of the areas of the Fermi surface contours for a particular wavevector, weighted by the energy of each contour. This relationship provides a fundamental explanation for the observed linear relationship between the areas of the Fermi surface contours and the components of the superfluid density in conventional superconductors. Additionally, it reveals that the topology of the Fermi surface contours for a particular wavevector determines the magnetic susceptibility in superconducting materials, with no need to assume a specific mechanism for spin-orbit coupling. This relationship can be used to calculate the magnetic susceptibility in materials with non-spherical electron energy spectra, as well as the distribution of paramagnetic moments in superconducting materials with multivalued Fermi surfaces, such as superconducting metals with magnetic moments attached to the electron pockets of their Fermi surfaces.

A conventional differential detection system is examined to determine if its performance can be enhanced by utilizing optimal threshold values in its decision-making process. The analysis, which is applicable to a wide range of signal types including continuous phase modulation, shows that the system's error rate can be reduced by upping the threshold for low signal-to-noise ratios and lowering it for high signal-to-noise ratios. The reasons behind this behavior are then explained by looking at the probability distributions of the detected signals. Next, simple yet effective methods for setting the threshold are presented and illustrated with numerical examples to show the resulting error rate improvements. These examples demonstrate significant error rate reductions of up to 6 dB in certain situations. The analysis stresses the importance of picking optimal threshold values in conventional differential detection systems and highlights the potential gains to be achieved from doing so.

The validity of the grand canonical ensemble for a system at constant pressure is potentially compromised if the system's compressibility is significantly high. A simulation method based on molecular dynamics or Monte Carlo can be modified to maintain the desired average pressure, but this approach doesn't provide a direct indicator of the legitimacy of the grand canonical ensemble. Here, we propose an alternative metric that can be used to assess the validity of the grand canonical ensemble through the fluctuation of the particle number in simulations held at constant pressure. A stronger signal of the legitimacy of the grand canonical ensemble is observed when simulations are performed over extended periods or with large numbers of particles. This proposed metric can serve as a critical assessment of the simulation's accuracy, in addition to the accuracy already ensured by satisfying the condition of constant pressure. This study further reveals that the particle number's fluctuations in simulations are directly proportional to the square root of the simulation box's volume and the duration of the simulation. This observation is in line with theoretical expectations based on the adiabatic expansion of harmonic oscillators and provides a realistic scenario for such simulations.

To better understand certain complex languages, it's proposed that neural models should be taught to recognize if-then relation hierarchies, which categorize relationships like "if it's day time, then the sun is visible" into more general patterns like "if condition A, then consequence B". This study supports the benefits of this approach, revealing that models trained to recognize these hierarchies with supervision can automatically acquire a sense of the relations' inherent hierarchy even when trained on text alone, without explicit labeling. This study also explores multiple ways to induce the models to learn the relations' hierarchy through semantic meaning, discovering that models rely heavily on word embeddings and contextualized embeddings in predicting the relations' hierarchy. Interestingly, models trained on a large, general corpus like Wikipedia can acquire a sense of the relations' hierarchy even without explicit labeling, unlike models trained on a smaller corpus like finitely labeled datasets. Additionally, the study demonstrates improved performance in predicting the hierarchy when models are forced to learn the relations in a particular order, indicating that models can become "confused" if presented with random orderings of the same relations.

Our new algorithm, dubbed NISQ-HHL, is an improved version of the HHL quantum algorithm, specifically tailored to operate effectively on noisy, intermediate-scale quantum machines. The original HHL algorithm solves systems of linear equations by leveraging the matrix inverse, but this approach proves too delicate for near-term quantum devices due to their inability to accurately implement inverse operations. The NISQ-HHL algorithm provides a more robust solution by utilizing the approximate inverse of a matrix, taking into account the quantum device's error potential. This implementation yields a more efficient use of quantum resources, enabling the solution of more complex linear systems on noisy quantum machines. The algorithm's capabilities are demonstrated through a meaningful example from the field of electrical impedance tomography.

To enhance the performance of state-of-the-art neural automated speech recognition systems, the bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) has been proposed as a way to strengthen the connection between speech representations and linguistic information. This attention mechanism allows for the exchange of information between the encoder and decoder, which enables the encoder to utilize knowledge from the decoder about the linguistic patterns in the input speech. As a result, the attention weights between the time-domain speech and the linguistic patterns can be two-way, which is the basis for the BiAM name. The BiAM is simple to implement, with only minor adjustments to the conventional transformer encoder network, and it demonstrates a significant improvement in recognition performance, especially for difficult speech data. The enhanced performance of BiAM is attributed to its ability to reduce the mismatch between the encoder and the training data, which is particularly beneficial when large amounts of supervised data are available. Additionally, the BiAM can be further optimized by reducing the attention weights between the encoder outputs and the linguistic patterns, which is a common strategy in neural network performance enhancement. The proposed BiAM method is tested in a 200-hour English recognition task and a 13-hour German recognition task, and the results show a significant improvement of up to 4.0% in word error rate (WER) compared to the conventional transformer encoder network.

This research examines the distribution of the initial $k_n$ parking spots in a random model from uniform distribution, where $n$ represents the total number of parking spaces. The main focus is on analyzing the differences between these initial parking spaces and desired uniform distribution, measured by total variation distance and Kolmogorov distance. The achievable rate of distributing the first $k_n$ parking spaces evenly is also analyzed in this study. Theoretical findings are accompanied by numerical data obtained through simulation testing. These simulations used random uniform generation to create instances of the random model.

Researchers are using nanoscale materials to create sensitive light measuring tools, and the properties of superconducting nanowires can be modified through metal oxide coating. Studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of these devices in high-resolution illumination intensity measurements. To further advance this technology, a theoretical model has been developed to predict the superconducting nanowire's electrical behavior under varying conditions. This model shows that the critical voltage, which marks the transition to superconductivity, can be adjusted by designing a feedback system that alters the applied voltage. By optimizing this feedback system, the nanowire's electrical characteristics can be tailored to meet specific performance requirements, enabling more precise illumination intensity measurements across a wider dynamic range.

Neural View Synthesis for videos seeks to generate images from new viewpoints given input video sequences. A recent approach called NVP-SVNX claims to enhance view synthesis by leveraging a dual representation of data. However, testing the method's effectiveness on videos from novel viewpoints is complicated due to limited dataset availability. To address this challenge, a novel Graph Attention Network for viewpoint synthesis is proposed, which efficiently explores different viewpoints without relying on extensive datasets. To further advance view synthesis, a dual representation used in NVP-SVNX is incorporated into the network design. By combining this representation with spatial and temporal attention mechanisms, the proposed network is capable of producing high-quality novel-viewpoint videos. To validate the method's performance, extensive experiments are conducted on various video datasets at the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV). Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate that the network generates scores that are significantly better in terms of SSIM and PSNR.

A crucial component in quantum communication systems is a beam splitter that can accurately manage the phase relationship between input and output photons. While traditional beam splitters are limited to managing first-order photonic modes, a newly proposed design can handle higher-order modes, potentially leading to the creation of entangled multi-photon states. The proposed phase beam splitter, with a specific design utilizing a non-equally spaced waveguide array, can achieve coherent manipulation of higher-order photonic modes, even in the presence of loss and nonlinear effects. The study demonstrates, using numerical methods, that a beam splitter with a specific design can successfully transfer a specific higher-order mode while minimizing mode-mixing, and it is further shown that this design can be effectively used to create entangled multi-photon states from a initial two-photon state. The generated entangled states meet the requirements for both Bell and Greenberger-Horne-Zimba states, and the study presents distinct methods for creating these states, along with the associated success probabilities and entanglement measures.

In quantum mechanics, the Elaydy-Newton approximation is an analytical method for generating periodic transformations of functions, and and its applications in quantum mechanics are particularly effective in processing complex energy spectra. This document is the first in a series of papers that will detail the Elaydy-Newton approximation's applications in analyzing the resonance mass spectra of hadrons. Specifically, this paper demonstrates how the Elaydy-Newton approximation can be used to analyze the mass spectra of meson and baryon resonances by applying a simple harmonic oscillator potential with different spin-orbit interactions. By using the approximation's properties, we can decompose the Hamiltonian into a direct sum of individual components, each representing a distinct physical phenomenon that affects the mass spectra in a distinct way. This includes the effects of the harmonic oscillator, spin-orbit interaction, as well as the linear and curvature Ralph-Schwinger corrections. Notably, this method allows us to categorize the mass spectra of all hadron states into three categories, each characterized by a specific type of energy distribution. This classification is in line with the IWE representation and provides a clear physical understanding of the energy spectra. Additionally, this method offers a direct solution to the eigenequation, which can be used to calculate the mass of each hadron state, as well as its corresponding quantum numbers. The rapid spread of COVID-19 pandemic prompted researchers to mathematically model its evolution using stochastic epidemic models. Among these models, the model that accounts for aerosol-driven transmission has gained significant attention. A particular model, known as the stochastic population model, assumes that aerosols evenly distribute throughout the population, suspend above it, or are trapped within it, providing the basis for its equations. To facilitate comparison with other models, the stochastic population model's predictions for aerosol-filled airspaces around infected individuals were compared to more intricate models featuring multiple particle populations. These comparisons showed that the stochastic population model accurately replicates the results of those other models, especially in maintaining similar particle size distributions. Furthermore, it was observed that the model that includes suspension loses its accuracy in predicting aerosol concentrations in close proximity to an infected individual, whereas the model featuring multiple populations fails to do so, despite delivering precise predictions over longer periods.

The Hall effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers has been investigated and compared to an ideal metallic system. Research indicates that the scattering mechanism is affected by the type of Bismuth layer present. When the number of Bismuth layers is odd, a anomalous increase in the carrier concentration is observed and explained by the presence of armchair-type interfaces. This is further supported by the presence of a positive ordinate intercept in the carrier concentration versus layer number plots. Additionally, layers of even number parity exhibit carrier concentrations more in line with the ideal metallic case, displaying no significant deviation from expected behavior. This unique phenomenon is attributed to the type of interface formed within the multilayer structure and has important implications for the understanding of carrier behavior in Cobalt/Bismium multilayers, particularly in relation to magnetic properties governed by carrier concentration at the Cobalt/Bismium interface.

This study examines the complex nature of Zitterbewegung in N-dimensional free and harmonic oscillator Schrödinger equations, particularly those with time-like and space-like non-local potentials. The analysis shows that the potential's nature can change depending on the fractional parameter α, particularly from space-like to time-like or vice versa. The research also explores the effects of varying α on the energy spectrum of both systems.

A recent neural network optimization technique involves constraining the $p$-norm of weight updates to achieve a desired Lipschitz constant, providing a useful regularization method, particularly in training neural networks to be fair and robust. This study investigates the impact of employing different $p$-norms in neural network optimization, specifically looking at $l_1$, $l_2$, and $l_p$-norms with $p=1.5$. The primary objective is to determine if there are significant performance differences when using these $l_p$-norms and if the optimal choice of $p$ leads to improved results. To thoroughly examine this issue, the research involves creating a flexible neural network optimization framework that can accommodate a wide range of $p$-norms and accurately tracks the underlying optimization problem. Theoretical analysis reveals that the choice of $p$-norm affects the convergence rate of the optimizer. To validate the proposed framework's performance, a thorough experimental investigation is conducted on a range of datasets, revealing that the best choice of $p$-norm, specifically $p=1.5$, yields improved results when compared to the commonly employed $l_1$ and $l_2$-norms. The study's findings and the developed neural network optimization framework can be used in scenarios where neural network optimization is sensitive to the choice of $p$-norm, such as in the constrained learning framework.

This paper provides an enhanced signal modeling for the search of vector leptoquarks at the LHC, using the NLO$+$PS methodology. Our primary focus is on the production of single and pair vector leptoquarks within the Standard Model, utilizing the MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO framework to generate results at the NLO level for the sub-processes and matching them with the parton shower for the parent processes. A study of the effects of different choices for the matching criteria, generator parameters, and jet clustering algorithms on the distribution of events is presented, along with a comparison of NLO$+$PS and FxFy merged samples using MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO and the impact of the generator parameters on the distribution of events, particularly in the presence of large multi-jet final states. In order to facilitate the incorporation of these results into experimental analyses, event weights in the form of histograms are provided for pair and single vector leptoquark productions, along with predictions for the most relevant processes at the 13 TeV LHC.

We propose a deep-neural-network (DNN) framework that enhances low-dose PET images using MRI information. This DNN framework, consisting of two layers, first learns to eliminate noise and restore high-dose PET images, then refines its output using paired examples. Training on paired data isn't always feasible due to the high costs and challenges associated with acquiring it, particularly in the field of nuclear medicine where PET and MRI scans aren't usually taken simultaneously. To address this, we utilize unpaired MRI and PET scans, leveraging a cycle-consistent GAN (CAGAN) DNN trained on separate datasets without needing paired examples. This allows us to develop a noise-reduction DNN, substitutable in the framework without compromising performance. Utilizing unpaired MRI data facilitates widespread applicability to various clinical scenarios. We validate our method by applying it to head and neck data with both low-dose and standard-dose PET scans available, and also to pancreatic data with only standard-dose PET scans available for comparison with state-of-the-art methods.

Recently introduced contextualized language models have significantly improved neural coreference resolution performance. To understand the effectiveness of these models, we re-run a range of coreference resolution experiments and contextualized embedding tests on the same data, utilizing the latest models and training data available today. Our findings reveal that contextualized embeddings are highly sensitive to the linguistic context and consistently reflect fundamental grammatical properties, including thematic relationship patterns. When fed into a neural network coreference resolver, these models achieve near-perfect performance on a range of tasks, including identifying elliptical subjects in English, based on gold standard coreference annotations. Our research also explores the relationship between coreference resolution and the theoretical framework of centering theory, revealing that contextualized embeddings accurately capture key notions, including the level of integration between an entity and its surrounding context. Despite the strong performance of neural network coreference resolvers, our experiments demonstrate that they are prone to large errors when dealing with non-standard coreference patterns, such as appositive relations. To address this limitation, we propose a simple adjustment to the neural network coreference resolver, which includes a globally shared embedding layer to capture general linguistic properties, resulting in a network that is significantly less prone to coreference errors, particularly with appositive relations.

Enabling location services and efficient navigation is crucial for users of public transportation, but providing updates on their location is challenging for transit networks since users don't remain connected for long periods. Once connected, determining a user's location becomes a complex problem due to limited data available before the short-lived connection is broken. In an effort to address this challenge, this research introduces a novel method to estimate a user's distance from their current location based on a brief interaction with a mobile app. This is achieved by training a machine learning model using a set of WiFi fingerprints with associated geographic coordinates in an offline map data base. By leveraging nearby accessible WiFi signals during a brief connection, the app can provide a rough estimate of the user's location and create a circle of possible locations on the map, which can be used to guide navigation even after the connection is lost. This research also explores multiple machine learning techniques and evaluates their performance under various scenarios to provide efficient and accurate location estimates. Experimental results show that using just 16 randomly selected training points from a large database of 12000 fingerprints is sufficient to achieve a high estimation accuracy.

As particle accelerators reach higher energies, the need for more efficient acceleration methods grows. Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs) that recycle energy from tail particles by firing at the front end can accelerate particles at up to thirty times the rate of traditional linacs while producing lower radiation levels. However, beam-RF interactions pose a challenge as particles approaching the end of their path may not reach the desired energy, thus requiring multiple filling procedures. The impact of fill patterns on beam dynamics is not thoroughly documented. This study investigates how different fill procedures affect beam-RF interactions, identifies patterns that increase the threshold current, and determines how varying beam energy, fill patterns, and RF phase affects this threshold. The results show that the threshold current can be improved by ten to a hundred times through appropriate fill procedures, and that the choice of fill procedure depends on the acceleration method, whether it's single-pass or multi-pass.

Using the color-ordered vertex (CEV) approach, the two-gluon vertex for the general QCD theory has been reconstructed from low-order interactions. This representation enables the derivation of a specific two-gluon amplitude that is constituent of a six-gluon MHV heptagon function in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. A comparable derivation of the two-gluon vertex for the N=4 theory, based on the SYM four-gluon amplitude, allows for a deeper understanding of the vertex's properties. This reveals a fundamental relationship between the two-gluon vertex and the dual conformal bitraceless operator of the N=4 theory's two-gluon amplitude. A natural extension of the CEV in QCD to three gluons is also explored.

Researchers are beginning to study the properties of polymer brushes in various surface curvatures, but accurately simulating stretched polymers in curved surfaces remains challenging due to rapid increases in computational costs with the number of particles. This study employs primitive chain methods to efficiently model polymer brushes in curved surfaces and then maps the results to a single-chain confederation method for greater accuracy. The primary focus is on examining the effects of surface curvature on the free energy of stretching in polymer brushes across a range of curvatures, from mildly concave to strongly convex. The study demonstrates that the single-chain confederation method accurately reproduces simulation results from the primitive chain method across diverse surface curvatures and regimes of chain density. The findings indicate that the free energy of stretching exhibits a non-monotonous change with increasing surface curvature. In very curved surfaces, both simulation methods reveal that the distribution of force generation within the brush layer becomes highly asymmetric, with significant implications for the architecture of polymer brushes in highly curved surfaces.

Inspired by the concept of metric dimension in graphs, we investigate similar properties in graphs derived from original graphs through a transformation that involves geodesic distance. Specifically, for any graph G and a positive number k, we define a truncated version of G, denoted as γ_k(G), which consists of the vertices of G that are within a distance of k from some initial set of seeds in G. We then explore how the size of the smallest seed set for γ_k(G) changes as the value of k varies. We show that this value can serve as a threshold for detecting a specific type of clique cover in graphs and provides a more general approach to solving a variety of other graph division problems. Additionally, this value can serve as a distance-based counterpart to the celebrated k-vertex cover problem in graphs. We provide a more in-depth analysis of this threshold value by investigating its behavior in relation to specific types of graphs and present a computational method for determining the metric dimension of these derived graphs.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) exhibit complex variability across multiple timescales, and long-term monitoring observations necessitate a broad spectrum analysis to determine variability characteristics. Nonetheless, spectroscopic observations, although rich in information, are frequently hampered by the need to allocate time for high-energy band observations for notable variability features like BLRs, where a lack of signal precludes firm detection. Furthermore, inherent limitations in traditional techniques, such as cross-correlation analysis, become apparent when attempting to detect minimal variability in dense dust absorbers like type 2 AGNs. In this research, we developed a non-parametric approach to determine the variability of the absorption line strength in a single spectrum without relying on previous assumptions about source variability or its cause. This method, which we referred to as the'signal-to-fluctuation' (S/F) technique, calculates a measure of variability in a single spectrum by examining the relationship between absorption line strength and its surrounding continuum. We applied the S/F technique to a dataset of 69 type 2 AGNs, analyzing the optical absorption lines of Mg II 1210, Al II 1210, and Al III 1216, and mapped their variability as a function of optical luminosity. The resulting distributions of variability were fit with a beta function for future use in simulated studies of AGN populations.

The Myerson mechanism for assigning licenses in a spectrum market based on valuations from bipartite matchings provides an efficient way to allocate non-overlapping frequencies. However, the lack of considerate matching algorithms limiting the number of frequencies a buyer can obtain for a given set of non-negative values makes the myerson mechanism lacking in scalability. In contrast, the gukhareswert algorithm is highly adaptable as it can handle large numbers of frequencies a buyer may be willing to pay for. Although the algorithm yields a near-optimal solution in a significant percentage of cases, it may also produce outcomes significantly worse than the myerson mechanism due to the need for additional spectrum reallocation, resulting in degraded allocation efficiency. The current study demonstrates how leveraging the gukhareswert algorithm can simplify the process of finding more feasible solutions for a wide range of NP-complete problems, including the spectrum market assignment task. The proposed approach generates a wide range of feasible solutions when considering a set of integer linear equations with variables representing time periods, but it can be challenging to determine if the generated solutions are near-optimal. The study also addresses how to direct the algorithm towards producing more efficient solutions, as well as how to apply the algorithm in a way that reduces the likelihood of generating inefficient solutions efficiently. The impact of these approaches is evaluated through experimental means, and the resulting data is analyzed to better understand the factors influencing the algorithm's performance.
