Firstly, we demonstrate that any formally developed mathematical system is inherently unable to completely and accurately identify all its own provably true statements, especially those that pertain to basic arithmetic. Secondly, within such a system, there always exists at least one unprovable statement that is, in fact, true. This improved incompleteness theorem, when applied to a formally developed mathematical system that is capable of modeling basic arithmetic, demonstrates a critical enhancement to its original counterpart. This upgrade is achieved without reliance on any additional, non-trivial, or more rigorous forms of set theory, thus avoiding a common criticism. This result is particularly significant because it represents the most fundamental and widely accepted application of Godel's first incompleteness theorem.

This talk focuses on a theoremic aspect of functions that are single-valued and come from a specific type of extension in higher dimensional spaces. Beginning with a brief overview of Hadamard's three circles theorem, the discussion explores recent developments in generalizing this concept to functions in higher dimensional spaces, specifically in the context of Clark's monogenic functions. The discussion also delves into the application of these generalized functions to a problem of identification and recovery in a higher dimensional setting.

We present a novel Wasserstein GAN framework, specifically a conditional version, 
which produces posterior examples in image processing. The key characteristic of this GAN 
structure is a regularized version of the conditional Wasserstein distance, resulting 
in a discriminator equation that includes a non-regularizing component from the 
original unconditional Wasserstein GAN. Leveraging this property enables us to train 
this GAN using only a single set of training data. The resulting model is called 
CW-WGAN-1, whereas the version utilizing two sets of training data is termed 
CW-WGAN-2. Both CW-WGAN-1 and CW-WGAN-2 produce high-quality generated images 
and, under certain conditions, are equivalent to the Bregman divergence-based GAN 
framework. Theoretical analysis of CW-WGAN-1 and CW-WGAN-2 is conducted, along 
with a discussion on the relationship with existing GAN structures. The proposed 
CW-WGAN-1 and CW-WGAN-2 methods are evaluated through generated image quality 
assessments using both the Fr\'{e}chet inception distance and the structural 
sensitivity analysis method. The experimental results demonstrate the superior 
performance of CW-WGAN-1 and CW-WGAN-2 compared to state-of-the-art GAN baselines.

This research paper examines linear fractional systems with time-invariant subspaces. It provides an in-depth look at the methods for determining if specific linear subspaces remain unchanged over time and their relationships with system modes. Additionally, the paper offers a new approach to solving the subspace identification problem. It includes mathematical proofs for key concepts and demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed method through numerical examples.

Using highly sensitive and precise radio telescopes at Arecibo and Green Bank, the pulse profiles of the oldest known pulsar, PSR B1133+16, were studied over 20 years and multiple frequencies. By processing a vast dataset of over 80 million recorded signals, researchers discovered an incredible 160 individual scattering screens interacting with the pulsar's light as it travels through space. Remarkably, 155 of these screenings were found to originate from a vast galactic disk, around 5,000 light-years from Earth, with distances varying significantly and offering a unique opportunity to precisely measure the distribution of dense particles in the Milky Way. This discovery provides a rare and fascinating insight into the pulsar's environment and a promising area for exploring the mysterious interstellar medium.

Thanks to its ability to tackle long-term dependencies, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have become the go-to choice for modeling time-series and speech signals. Yet, a critical shortcoming of traditional RNN architectures limits their effectiveness: they cannot model completely periodic signals, especially those with diverse frequencies, as demonstrated in songs with multiple melodic lines. To address this challenge, a cascaded network structure was recently proposed, which enables a specific type of RNN, called Phase-Reduced Neural Networks (PRNNs), to efficiently capture and replicate complex time domains containing multiple frequencies. In evaluating this PRNN model, a challenging task with diverse and constantly changing frequencies was created, specifically a song with multiple melodic lines played on a piano. The results showed that the PRNN network not only accurately learned and replicated this complex time domain but also demonstrated a high level of robustness in the face of significant modifications. In comparing the PRNN to other sophisticated time-domain modeling techniques, including a cascaded network, the current state-of-the-art method, a surprising contrast was observed: while the PRNN model yielded a significantly lower mean absolute error when replicating this specific song, its overall performance varied greatly when applied to other diverse time domains.

We introduce a concept called'shadows' within the bicategorical framework of topological Hochschild homology (THHH) and demonstrate how they are equivalent to the notion of cyclonic functors from the bicategory of algebras to the bicategory of modules. This connection enables a straightforward definition of THHH for bicategorical functors, which we then apply to establish a relationship between shadows and the functor that maps a functor to its THH, showing that this functor is fully determined by its shadow-related properties. This, in turn, leads to the existence of a universal cyclonic functor, resulting in the existence of a universal cyclonic module for each functor. This module comes equipped with a natural transformation connecting the original functor to the functor obtained by mapping along the universal cyclonic functor. This mapping functor is essentially the same as the functor that maps a functor to its THH, except it is defined within a broader bicategorical context. This enables us to define the top dimensional component of THH for a functor F, denoted as THH(F), by focusing solely on the properties of shadows, without relying on the specifics of F's underlying category. This approach allows for the generalization of THH to a wider category of functors, specifically those defined within a bicategorical context.

VGG-Sound Source is a comprehensive new dataset consisting of 24 different sound source classes, meticulously curated from 35 existing datasets totaling 2,500 hours of high-quality, real-world recordings. This benchmark, designed to facilitate the development and evaluation of source separation models, sets a higher standard than existing sound source isolation datasets. VGG-SS distinguishes itself from other datasets by being large in scale, all-around, and publicly accessible, offering a wide range of sounds, including both common and rare environments. Unlike many current source isolation models, the VGG-SS dataset does not rely on artificial mixtures, instead utilizing natural, unmanipulated sounds from various sources, including both single and multi-sound mixtures. This dataset comes with pre-trained models capable of both non-music and music source separation, achieving notable results on the VGG-SS benchmark with mean source-to-noise ratio (SNR) scores ranging from 3.5 to 7.5, and a mean signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain of 10.5 dB on the VGG-SS benchmark.

Previous works on graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in hyperbolic space have been limited by their slow convergence rates, inaccurate node feature representations, and the requirement for complete node adjacency information. To address these issues, we introduce the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which leverages a novel Lorentzian graph attention mechanism and a designed sampling strategy to enable fast and accurate node feature representations, without relying on complete adjacency information. We further prove that the LGCN learns from a specific distribution of Lorentzian manifolds, which facilitates an analysis of its performance. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets reveal that the LGCN outperforms existing hyperbolic GCNs and comparable Euclidean baselines by significant margins.

This PhD study focuses on the analysis and development of numerical methods for solving a specific inverse problem associated with a time-dependent heat equation. The primary goal is to determine the initial temperature distribution based on temperature measurements taken at a single point over a fixed time period. The underlying strategy involves creating a sequence of steady heat equation problems, each set in a successively smaller domain, whose solutions converge to the desired initial condition. The study's initial contribution is to establish an observability inequality for a family of steady heat equation problems defined on growing domains. This is achieved by employing a compactness method, assuming the domain's growth satisfies a specific condition. The second part of the study presents two numerical methods for solving the inverse problem. The first is a gradient-based method, where the observability inequality is used to establish the differentiability of a key operator. The second is a nonlinear algebraic solver for a discrete inverse problem. The study assumes a highly resolved finite element discretization and shows that the corresponding nonlinear algebraic system has a unique solution in a certain Banach space. The approach is extended to include uncertainty analysis, enabled by the use of random coefficient representations and the application of the Bertrand-Roux mass finite element method. The study's final contribution involves numerical experiments, conducted on a complex domain with a curved boundary, and featuring temperature measurements affected by noise. The purpose of these experiments is to demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed approach and evaluate the performance of the methods developed throughout the study.

The Tsallis distribution has been extensively applied in various physical sciences and has also found a home in social systems, finance, and biology. Despite its utility, the underlying reasons for its widespread adoption remain unclear, as does the fundamental basis for deviating from the Gibbs distribution. An information-thermodynamic approach may provide a framework for understanding the Tsallis distribution within complex systems. By considering information sources with non-additive entropy, the Tsallis distribution can serve as a natural generalization of the Gibbs distribution. This approach has already been successfully applied in analyzing the origins of the Tsallis distribution in random matrix theory, gravitational physics, and financial modeling. Notably, this approach has not been explored in the context of acoustic systems or phonon statistics. This study fills this knowledge gap by first introducing the information-thermodynamic approach to understanding the Tsallis distribution in acoustic systems and then applies it to the harmonic oscillator with a non-additive entropy, explaining the deviations from the Gibbs distribution in phonon statistics.

This article formalizes the free massless gravitational theory in a specific type of metric formulation and systematically examines the inclusion of a mass term in linearized gravity for both its physical and geometric interpretations. The analysis across various formulations reveals the absence of a true mass term for the physical gravitational degrees of freedom but results in a conversion between the two polarization states for the massive component of the perturbed graviton, effectively creating a mixture of massless and massive degrees of freedom. The article also explores the Fierz-Pauli formulation, often presented as a starting point for massive gravity theories, and reveals that it is actually a representation of the mass-component's four-dimensional degrees of freedom rather than a true inclusion of a mass term into the free gravity theory. The article ultimately shows that the Fierz-Pauli formulation can be reinterpreted as a curvilinear gravity theory and explains the underlying geometric reasoning for the specific form of its mass term.

For closed quantum systems with a finite number of levels, we establish a comprehensive framework of Hamiltonian dynamics centered on quantum equilibrium states. This framework, complementing the existing focus on quantum dynamics through generators of unitary transformations, is framed by its natural connection to classical dynamics. Specifically, we identify four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics that mirror distinct classical dynamics: (I) time-reversal symmetry, (II) symmetry under phase-space parity, (III) symmetry under time-reversal combined with phase-space parity, and (IV) asymmetric dynamics. For closed quantum systems with a continuous energy spectrum, we construct quantum equilibrium states as functionals of classical trajectories, labeled by the N-dimensional simplex, and systematically explore the properties of these constructed states. Furthermore, we establish the existence and uniqueness of quantum equilibrium states corresponding to specific classical dynamics.

A common misconception about negative temperature is that it requires a continuous, complex energy spectrum to manifest. We demonstrate that negative temperature can be effectively illustrated using a basic two-level system framework, where energy levels are distinct and represent a fundamental concept, especially when the population inversion reaches a point where the system's entropy is zero but its temperature becomes negative. By examining the behavior of an idealized two-level system under various heating sources, we can observe both positive and negative temperatures emerging, and even see how the system's statistics can mimic those of a Bose-Einstein condensate. In one specific scenario where the system is in contact with a heat bath of harmonic oscillators, we show how the system's behavior can mimic the formation of a BEC, yet with a key difference where the system's temperature can become negative due to population inversion, a phenomenon that can be distinguished from a true BEC formation.

In a theory where a minimal dark sector interacts with the standard model, not through fundamental forces, a particular type of symmetry called dark parity symmetry can hold if a specific condition is met. This paper delves into a type of neutrino mass generation called the "seesaw mechanism" and explores how a minimal dark sector affects the stability of the vacuum and the consistency of dark parity symmetry. Although the effects on the vacuum stability and the consistency of dark parity symmetry are generally small in the case of neutrinos, this paper shows that this is not unique and that a similar pattern of behavior can be observed in other particles, such as charged fermions and heavy scalar particles. By incorporating a minimal dark sector into a theory that violates dark parity symmetry, this paper demonstrates that the dark sector can either restore dark parity symmetry or violate it further, all while generating tiny neutrino masses.

Researchers who study transition metal oxides often need to refer to spin-orbit coupling, which arises from the interaction between a specific kind of polarization of electrons and the crystal that contains them. This kind of coupling can be very strong in certain materials and has a significant impact on their physical properties. However, calculating it accurately is complicated due to the interactions between the electrons and the crystal, the movements of the electrons within the material's chemical bonds, and the specific properties of the material's energy band structure. In a new study, an improved method was developed to calculate the effective spin-orbit coupling in materials by accounting for both the strong interactions between the electrons and the distortions of the crystal lattice. This approach can be applied to the study of magnetic interactions in materials with strong spin-orbit coupling and can be used to simulate experimental data from techniques that rely on simulated Scattering, such as X-ray Magnetic Scattering. By applying this method to simulations of X-ray Magnetic Scattering, the study provides a detailed understanding of how the distribution of electrons within a material's chemical bonds affects the scattering patterns, which can be compared to experimental data from various materials.

We establish a deeper connection between the relative $I$-functions of toric complete intersections and those of hypersurfaces. Specifically, for a toric complete intersection whose divisor is smooth, we show that the associated relative $I$-functions can be expressed in terms of the relative $I$-functions of hypersurfaces within its defining polynomial ring. Moreover, this expression takes the form of a combinatorial sum, where each term is either a product of certain components from the relative $I$-functions of hypersurfaces or a product of components derived directly from the relative $I$-function of the complete intersection itself. Furthermore, we provide a computational method to determine the components of the relative $I$-functions for toric complete intersections, and we illustrate this method through examples of both plane curves and higher-dimensional spaces.

A growing number of medical applications involves using generative models, particularly text-to-image models, which can manipulate latent code to alter the underlying structure of generated images. Despite their utility, it's crucial to assess these models' semantic representation of medical conditions. In this work, we explore the underlying semantic structure of Condition-specific Text-to-Image Models (CTIMs) through code-to-text reverse generation. Our study reveals both a strong and distorted relationship between the latent code and accompanying text, which we analyzed by modifying the latent code and observing the impact on nearby codes and the associated images. Our findings show that modifying the latent code can either preserve a local semantic context or disrupt the representation, depending on the magnitude of change. Consequently, extreme code alterations can result in an exchange of conditions in the represented images. Our analysis also uncovered three distinct regimes of code modification: a free movement regime where the relationship between code and condition is loose, a diffusion regime marked by an gradual spread of the condition, and a snap regime where the condition suddenly changes. Notably, our study reveals that the latent space is not a linear representation of conditions but rather a nonlinear, non-Euclidean structure. Our work also includes a computational example of code manipulation in a synthetic lung image, which can be beneficial for medical education.

A newly developed application called ViDaExpert is presented, which is an easy-to-use visual data explorer designed to navigate complex, high-dimensional spaces with multiple attributes and data points. This visualization tool maps each attribute to a specific axis, allowing for the creation of multiple feature spaces where the relationships between attributes and data points can be examined and visualized three-dimensionally. A distinctive aspect of ViDaExpert is its ability to project unseen data points into these visualized feature spaces for analysis. This capability is made possible through the use of stochastic dimension reduction techniques, which enable the evaluation of how well a subset of attributes predicts the characteristics of unseen data points. By integrating this method with visualization, ViDaExpert can display a metric that represents the quality of these visualized feature spaces. This allows users to identify optimal sets of attributes that provide the clearest and most accurate visual representation of the underlying structure of their data.
